fontlab.reference:
## Architecture

The FontLab Python API is a C++/Python binding layer:

```
Python Script
    ↓ fontlab module
    ↓ C++ model objects
fl* classes (flNode, flContour, flShape, flLayer, flGlyph, flPackage…)
    ↓ fontgate (fg*)
fgGlyph, fgFont, fgContour…
```

The class articles document registered names, member kinds, calling conventions and property access. Some APIs depend on build flags. The separate `fontgate` module and inherited PythonQt/Qt APIs are outside this inventory.

`CurrentFont()` returns `fgFont`, and `CurrentGlyph()` returns `fgGlyph`. Use `fl.flPackage(fg_font)` or `fl.flGlyph(fg_glyph)` when calling the model APIs described by the `fl*` guides. Constructing a wrapper from an existing model object does not imply an independent geometry copy; use the appropriate `clone()` operation when a separate object is needed.

## Type Conventions

Throughout the documentation, types use these conventions:

| Type | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `str` | Python string (C++ `QString`) |
| `float` | Python float (C++ `double`) |
| `int` | Python integer |
| `bool` | Python bool |
| `QPointF` | Qt 2D point; use `PythonQt.QtCore.QPointF` unless the specific overload documents tuple conversion |
| `QRectF` | Qt rectangle; use `PythonQt.QtCore.QRectF` unless the specific overload documents tuple conversion |
| `QTransform` | 3×3 matrix — passed as a `QTransform`-like object |
| `QColor` | Qt color; use `PythonQt.QtGui.QColor` unless the specific overload documents tuple conversion |
| `list(T)` | Python `list` of type T |
| `T/None` | Returns T or Python `None` |

## Calling conventions and inherited members

Registered methods take positional arguments unless their class article explicitly lists keyword support. Optional values shown as `name=default` in signatures do not by themselves imply keyword support. `flNode` documents its keyword-capable methods. Value-wrapper constructors document their own field-keyword initialization.

Inherited registrations are documented in the base class article; each class article names its binding base where applicable. C++ inheritance alone does not guarantee that a base member is exposed in Python. Binding annotations record declared signatures and can be incomplete; implementation notes in the class articles qualify known differences.

fontlab.AccentInfo.reference:
An accent-placement result returned by `flPackage.getAccentsInfo(layer, pin)`. It combines a candidate accent layer with the transform needed to position it.

`AccentInfo()` constructs a value wrapper. Positional fields follow `(layer, offset)`; field keywords are supported. `asTuple()` and `asDict()` return snapshots. Indexing, item assignment and `len()` use the same field order. For placement results, prefer values supplied by flPackage.getAccentsInfo rather than inventing an offset.

fontlab.AccentInfo.offset.reference: Placement transform; this is a matrix, not an `(x, y)` pair.

fontlab.CurveEx.reference:
A single Bézier segment.

## What is CurveEx?

When you look at a letterform's outline in FontLab, you see a series of nodes connected by curve segments. Internally, each of those curve segments is stored as a **CurveEx** object. It holds four points — the two on-curve endpoints and the two off-curve control points (the "handles") — and provides mathematical operations on that single Bézier segment.

Most designers won't use `CurveEx` directly unless they are writing geometry-processing scripts. The most common way to encounter CurveEx objects is through `flShapeData.segments`, which gives you all segments of a shape as a flat list for bulk processing.

## Tutorial

```python
import fontlab as fl

# ============================================================
# Get the segments from a shape.
# flShapeData.segments gives you a flat list of all Bézier
# segments for every contour in the shape.
# ============================================================

font  = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font['S']   # 'S' has nice smooth curves to inspect
layer = glyph.layers[0]
shape = layer.shapes[0]

segs = shape.shapeData.segments
print(f"Total Bézier segments in 'S': {len(segs)}")

# ============================================================
# Print the basic geometry of each segment.
# Each segment goes from p0 (start node) to p1 (end node),
# with bcp0 and bcp1 as the off-curve control handles.
# ============================================================

for i, seg in enumerate(segs):
    if not seg.empty():
        length = seg.fastLength()
        kind   = "line" if seg.countPoints == 1 else "curve"
        print(f"Segment {i} ({kind}): "
              f"p0=({seg.p0.x():.0f},{seg.p0.y():.0f}) → "
              f"p1=({seg.p1.x():.0f},{seg.p1.y():.0f})  "
              f"length≈{length:.0f}")

# ============================================================
# Find all smooth joins in the glyph.
# A smooth join is where two consecutive segments share a
# node whose handles are collinear — no corner, just a smooth
# transition. This is what you see as a "smooth node" in the UI.
# ============================================================

smooth_count = 0
for i in range(1, len(segs)):
    if segs[i].smooth(segs[i-1]):
        smooth_count += 1
print(f"\nSmooth joins: {smooth_count} out of {len(segs)-1}")

# ============================================================
# Find potential missing extremum nodes.
# An extremum is a topmost/bottommost/leftmost/rightmost point.
# If a curve reaches its extreme inside a segment (not at a
# node), that is a "missing extremum" — important for correct
# PostScript hinting and clean vector export.
# ============================================================

print("\nPotential missing extrema:")
missing = 0
for i in range(1, len(segs)):
    if segs[i].extremum(segs[i-1]):
        missing += 1
        print(f"  At node {i}: ({segs[i].p0.x():.0f}, {segs[i].p0.y():.0f})")

if missing == 0:
    print("  None found — all extrema have nodes.")
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Count curve vs line segments across a glyph

```python
import fontlab as fl

font  = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font['O']
layer = glyph.layers[0]

curves = 0
lines  = 0
for shape in layer.shapes:
    for seg in shape.shapeData.segments:
        if not seg.empty():
            if seg.countPoints == 1:
                lines  += 1
            else:
                curves += 1

print(f"'O': {curves} curve segments, {lines} line segments")
```

### Check if all smooth nodes are actually smooth

```python
import fontlab as fl

font  = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font['n']
layer = glyph.layers[0]

for shape in layer.shapes:
    segs = shape.shapeData.segments
    for i in range(1, len(segs)):
        node_idx = segs[i].leftIdx
        # Compare the geometric smoothness of the join:
        is_smooth = segs[i].smooth(segs[i-1])
        print(f"  Node {node_idx}: geometrically smooth = {is_smooth}")
```

fontlab.CurveEx.applyTransform.reference: Moves, scales, or rotates all four points of this segment using the transform matrix `tx`. Modifies the segment in place. Call `updateBRect()` afterwards to refresh the cached bounding box.

fontlab.CurveEx.bcp0.reference: The **off-curve handle adjacent to p0** (the outgoing handle). Moving this changes how the curve leaves `p0`.

fontlab.CurveEx.bcp1.reference: The **off-curve handle adjacent to p1** (the incoming handle). Moving this changes how the curve arrives at `p1`.

fontlab.CurveEx.bcv0.reference: The direction vector from `p0` to `bcp0`. A read-only derived value. Useful for normalising the handle direction.

fontlab.CurveEx.bcv1.reference: The direction vector from `p1` to `bcp1`. Read-only.

fontlab.CurveEx.brect.reference: The cached axis-aligned bounding rectangle of this segment. Update with `updateBRect()` after changing points.

fontlab.CurveEx.contourIx.reference: Index of the parent contour within its shape.

fontlab.CurveEx.countPoints.reference: Number of on-curve points in this segment: `2` for a cubic Bézier, `1` for a straight line segment.

fontlab.CurveEx.empty.reference: Returns `True` if this segment is degenerate — all four points coincide, or the segment has not been initialised. A segment with `countPoints == 1` (a line) is not considered empty.

fontlab.CurveEx.extremum.reference: Checks whether the shared node between this segment and `prev` is at a local extremum — the topmost, bottommost, leftmost, or rightmost point of the curve at that junction. Returns `True` if it is an extremum. Use this when auditing a glyph for missing extremum nodes.

fontlab.CurveEx.fastLength.reference: Computes a quick approximation of the arc length (the actual measured length along the curve). The approximation uses the chord length plus a fraction of the handle distances — it is fast and good enough for most layout purposes, but not numerically exact.

fontlab.CurveEx.improve.reference: Adjusts the off-curve control points to improve the visual quality of the curve, targeting the given `curvature` factor. A factor of `1.0` preserves the approximate arc length while making the curve more balanced. Returns `True` if the points were changed.

fontlab.CurveEx.leftIdx.reference: Index of the left node (`p0`) within the parent contour's node list.

fontlab.CurveEx.p0.reference: The **left (start) on-curve point** of this segment. This is the node at the beginning of the segment.

fontlab.CurveEx.p1.reference: The **right (end) on-curve point** of this segment. The node at the end.

fontlab.CurveEx.paramT.reference: The parametric position (0..1) of the most recently queried point on this segment. Set by hit-test operations; read to find where on the segment a query point landed.

fontlab.CurveEx.rightIdx.reference: Index of the right node (`p1`) within the parent contour's node list.

fontlab.CurveEx.smooth.reference: Checks whether this segment and the previous segment `prev` join smoothly (G1 continuity — the tangent direction is the same on both sides of the shared node). Returns `True` if smooth. Use this to find which nodes in an outline are already smooth before applying a smoothing script.

fontlab.CurveEx.smoothCurvature.reference: Returns a new `CurveEx` with its handles adjusted for smooth curvature continuity (G2) between this segment and `c1`. If `complete` is `True`, both ends of the returned segment are adjusted; if `False`, only the join end is adjusted.

fontlab.CurveEx.split.reference: Splits this segment at its stored `paramT` value into two new segments. The two result segments are written into the two `CurveEx` arguments passed in. Returns `True` on success.

fontlab.CurveEx.updateBRect.reference: Recomputes the segment's cached bounding rectangle from its current point positions. Always call this after manually changing `p0`, `p1`, `bcp0`, or `bcp1`.

- `emPreviewText`: Preview text mode
- `emEditOutline`: Edit outline mode

fontlab.ExportControl.reference:
Font export configuration.

## What is ExportControl?

When you export a font (File → Export Font As), FontLab reads a set of parameters: which export profile (OpenType PS, Variable TTF, etc.), where to put the files, how to handle conflicts. `ExportControl` lets scripts access and modify these parameters programmatically.

The most common use is in automation scripts that export many fonts to a predictable location: set the profile, set the folder, set `conflictMode = 0` (overwrite), then call the export command. This is the scripting equivalent of clicking through the Export Font dialog.

## Tutorial

```python
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import ExportControl

# ============================================================
# Set up a clean export configuration for batch use.
# This is the scripting equivalent of filling in the
# Export Font As dialog and clicking OK.
# ============================================================

ec = ExportControl()
ec.init()   # always start from clean defaults

# Choose the export profile:
ec.profileName = "OpenType PS"   # OTF with CFF outlines

# Tell FontLab where to put the exported files:
ec.destinationMode   = 1                      # 1 = custom folder
ec.destinationFolder = "/tmp/exported_fonts/" # absolute path

# Don't ask about conflicts — just overwrite:
ec.conflictMode = 0   # 0 = overwrite existing files

# Export the full font (not just selected glyphs):
ec.contentMode = 0   # 0 = full font

# Organise output by family name (all styles in one folder):
ec.groupFamily = True

print(f"Export config: '{ec.profileName}' → '{ec.destinationFolder}'")

# ============================================================
# Save settings so they persist for next time.
# ============================================================
ec.store()
print("Settings saved.")

# ============================================================
# Load previously saved settings and adjust one field.
# Useful if you want to preserve most settings but change the
# profile for this run.
# ============================================================
ec2 = ExportControl()
if ec2.load():
    print(f"Loaded profile: '{ec2.profileName}'")
    ec2.profileName = "Variable TTF"  # override just the profile
    print(f"Changed to: '{ec2.profileName}'")
else:
    print("No saved settings found — starting from defaults.")
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Export to OTF and UFO in one pass

```python
from fontlab import ExportControl

# Export OTF:
ec = ExportControl()
ec.init()
ec.profileName       = "OpenType PS"
ec.destinationMode   = 1
ec.destinationFolder = "/tmp/exports/otf/"
ec.conflictMode      = 0
ec.store()
# fl.ExportFont(ec)   # call the export command

# Export UFO:
ec.profileName       = "UFO"
ec.destinationFolder = "/tmp/exports/ufo/"
ec.store()
# fl.ExportFont(ec)
```

### Export only selected glyphs

```python
from fontlab import ExportControl

ec = ExportControl()
ec.init()
ec.profileName    = "OpenType PS"
ec.destinationMode = 1
ec.destinationFolder = "/tmp/subset_export/"
ec.contentMode    = 1   # 1 = selected glyphs only
ec.conflictMode   = 0
```

fontlab.ExportControl.conflictMode.reference: How to handle existing files with the same name. `0` = silently overwrite. `1` = skip (do not overwrite). `2` = ask the user each time. For batch scripts, use `0` to overwrite or `1` to skip safely.

fontlab.ExportControl.contentMode.reference: What to include in the export. `0` = full font. `1` = selected glyphs only. `2` = current master only.

fontlab.ExportControl.contentName.reference: Human-readable name for the current export-content selection.

fontlab.ExportControl.destinationMode.reference: Where to write the exported files. `0` = same folder as the source file. `1` = the folder specified in `destinationFolder`. `2` = ask the user each time. For batch scripts, use `1` with a fixed path.

fontlab.ExportControl.groupFamily.reference: If `True`, all styles of the same font family are grouped into a family-named subfolder. Keeps your exported fonts tidy when exporting an entire type family at once.

fontlab.ExportControl.groupProfiles.reference: If `True`, files from different export profiles are grouped into profile-named subfolders within the destination. Useful when exporting both OTF and TTF from the same font.

fontlab.ExportControl.init.reference: Resets all properties to their factory default values. Call this at the start of an export script to start from a known state, so previously saved settings don't accidentally influence the batch run.

fontlab.ExportControl.load.reference: Loads previously stored settings from preferences. Returns `True` if settings were found. Use this to restore the user's last export configuration before modifying it in a script — you can load, then override just the fields you need.

fontlab.ExportControl.profileId.reference: The numeric ID of the export profile. Use `profileName` unless you know the exact numeric ID.

fontlab.ExportControl.profileName.reference: The name of the export profile — exactly as it appears in the export dialog. Examples: `"OpenType PS"`, `"OpenType TT"`, `"Variable TTF"`, `"UFO"`. Look up available profile names in FontLab's export dialog.

fontlab.ExportControl.store.reference: Saves the current settings to FontLab's preferences storage so they persist across application restarts. Equivalent to what FontLab does when you click OK in the export dialog. Useful at the end of a batch script to remember the last used settings.

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.reference:
A single font audit finding.

## What is FaBasic?

When you run FontLab's font audit (the grid of checkmarks in Font Window → Font Audit), the engine inspects every glyph for common outline problems: open contours, reversed winding, nearly-straight curves that should be lines, extremum nodes that are missing, and so on. Each detected problem is an `FaBasic` record.

In scripts, you access `FaBasic` records through `flAuditInfo.basic`. The most useful scripting workflow is:
1. Run the audit (open the Font Audit panel to populate results).
2. Iterate the findings via `flAuditInfo` objects.
3. For each auto-fixable finding (`canBeFixed == True`), call `fix()`.
4. Call `fl.Update()` to refresh the display.

*(Registered as `FaBasicPtr` in source; Python sees it as `FaBasic`)*

## Tutorial

```python
import fontlab as fl

# ============================================================
# The audit results are stored on flAuditInfo objects, which
# wrap FaBasic records. Access them through the canvas info
# system after running the audit.
#
# This example shows how to print and optionally auto-fix
# all audit findings for a specific glyph.
# ============================================================

font  = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font['S']   # try a glyph with complex curves

# Run the audit for this glyph's first layer:
layer = glyph.layers[0]

# Access audit results (method name may vary by version):
# audit_items = layer.auditResults()   # returns list of flAuditInfo

# For demonstration, we simulate what you would do with the results:
# for audit_info in audit_items:
#     b = audit_info.basic
#     print(f"Issue: {b.title}")
#     print(f"  Priority: {b.priority}")
#     print(f"  Location: ({b.location.x():.0f}, {b.location.y():.0f})")
#     print(f"  Report: {b.report}")
#     print(f"  Can be fixed: {b.canBeFixed}")
#
#     if b.canBeFixed:
#         result = b.fix()
#         if result:
#             print(f"  → Auto-fixed! Glyph '{result.name}' updated.")
#         else:
#             print(f"  → Fix returned Nothing.")

# ============================================================
# After fixing any issues, always update the display:
# ============================================================
fl.Update()
print("Audit review complete.")
```

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.canBeFixed.reference: `True` if calling `fix()` will automatically resolve this issue. `False` for issues that require manual intervention (e.g. a very complex curve that the auto-fixer doesn't know how to improve).

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.contour.reference: The contour this issue is associated with, or `Nothing` if the issue is at a higher level (e.g. a font-level metric problem).

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.fix.reference: Attempts to automatically fix the outline problem described by this record. For example: closes an open contour, corrects a reversed path direction, or adds a missing extremum node. Returns the modified `flGlyph` if the fix was applied, or `Nothing` if the issue cannot be auto-corrected (some issues require manual designer judgement). Always call `fl.Update()` after fixing to refresh the canvas.

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.id.reference: The numeric code identifying which audit rule produced this finding. Stable across FontLab versions.

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.location.reference: The glyph-space coordinates of where the issue is located. Use this with `flAuditInfo.glyphLocation()` to convert to canvas coordinates for drawing an indicator.

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.nodeIndex.reference: The index of the specific node involved in this issue within its contour. `-1` if the issue is not associated with a particular node. Use this with `contour.nodeAtIndex(nodeIndex)` to retrieve the problematic node.

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.priority.reference: The severity of this issue. Higher numbers are more important. Use this to sort issues by priority when generating a report.

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.report.reference: The full detailed description of the issue, including measurements, coordinate values, and fix recommendations. This is the text that FontLab shows in its audit panel.

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.title.reference: A brief, human-readable name for this type of issue, such as `"Open contour"`, `"Wrong direction"`, `"Almost flat curve"`. Use this in log output or a custom report.

fontlab.FaBasicPtr.vector.reference: A direction vector associated with the issue. For example, for a "node should move to extremum" issue, this vector points from the current position to the target extremum position.

fontlab.FontLayer.reference:
This auxiliary wrapper is registered by the module and accepts `FontLayer(package, name)`, with an `flPackage` and a string. Its binding registers no own methods or properties. The present constructor reads the string but does not use it to select a master.

For supported master access, use flPackage and its master-related members, or select a glyph's named flLayer. `FontLayer` should not be used as a substitute for selecting or editing a master.

fontlab.FontMetrics.reference:
Vertical metric values for one master.

## What is FontMetrics?

Every master in a font has a set of vertical metrics: how tall is the tallest letter, how far does the descender drop below the baseline, how tall are the lowercase letters, and so on. `FontMetrics` is a simple container that holds these six values for one master.

These are the values that determine the overall proportions of your design:
- **UPM** — the grid size. All other values are relative to this.
- **Ascender** — the top of tall lowercase letters like 'd', 'h', 'l'. Typically 70–80% of UPM.
- **Descender** — the bottom of descending letters like 'g', 'p', 'y'. Typically -20% to -30% of UPM (negative).
- **x-height** — the top of short lowercase letters like 'x', 'n', 'o'. Typically 45–55% of UPM.
- **Cap height** — the top of uppercase letters like 'H', 'I'. Typically 60–75% of UPM.
- **Line gap** — extra space between lines. Usually 0 for most text fonts.

You will use `FontMetrics` mainly to read or verify master-specific metrics in scripts. For the values exported into the OpenType tables, use `FontInfo` instead.

## Tutorial

```python
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import FontMetrics

font = fl.CurrentFont()

# ============================================================
# Read the vertical metrics from the first master.
# ============================================================

master = font.masters[0]
fm = FontMetrics(font, master)

print(f"Metrics for master '{master}':")
print(f"  UPM:        {fm.upm:.0f}")
print(f"  Ascender:   {fm.ascender:.0f}")
print(f"  Descender:  {fm.descender:.0f}")
print(f"  x-Height:   {fm.xHeight:.0f}")
print(f"  Cap Height: {fm.capsHeight:.0f}")
print(f"  Line Gap:   {fm.lineGap:.0f}")

# ============================================================
# Compute some useful ratios from the metrics.
# These ratios describe the proportions of the typeface.
# ============================================================

total_height = fm.ascender - fm.descender
x_ratio      = fm.xHeight   / fm.upm * 100
cap_ratio    = fm.capsHeight / fm.upm * 100

print(f"\nProportions:")
print(f"  Total height (asc-dsc): {total_height:.0f} units")
print(f"  x-height / UPM:         {x_ratio:.1f}%")
print(f"  Cap height / UPM:       {cap_ratio:.1f}%")

# ============================================================
# Check all masters have consistent x-height values.
# Inconsistent x-heights across masters cause problems in
# variable fonts.
# ============================================================

print("\nChecking x-height consistency across masters:")
x_heights = {}
for master_name in font.masters:
    fm = FontMetrics(font, master_name)
    x_heights[master_name] = fm.xHeight
    print(f"  [{master_name}] x-height = {fm.xHeight:.0f}")

values = list(x_heights.values())
if len(set(values)) == 1:
    print("✓ All masters have the same x-height.")
else:
    print(f"⚠ x-heights differ across masters!")
    for name, val in x_heights.items():
        print(f"    {name}: {val:.0f}")

# ============================================================
# Create a FontMetrics struct and set values manually.
# Useful when you want to compare or document intended values.
# ============================================================

target = FontMetrics(1000.0)   # 1000 UPM
target.ascender  =  730
target.descender = -270
target.xHeight   =  540
target.capsHeight = 710
target.lineGap   =   0

print(f"\nTarget metrics: "
      f"asc={target.ascender}  dsc={target.descender}  "
      f"xh={target.xHeight}  cap={target.capsHeight}")
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Print a metrics summary for every master

```python
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import FontMetrics

font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(f"{'Master':<20} {'UPM':>6} {'Asc':>6} {'Dsc':>6} {'xH':>6} {'Cap':>6}")
for master in font.masters:
    fm = FontMetrics(font, master)
    print(f"{master:<20} {fm.upm:>6.0f} {fm.ascender:>6.0f} "
          f"{fm.descender:>6.0f} {fm.xHeight:>6.0f} {fm.capsHeight:>6.0f}")
```

### Check that ascender + |descender| ≤ UPM

```python
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import FontMetrics

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for master in font.masters:
    fm = FontMetrics(font, master)
    total = fm.ascender + abs(fm.descender)
    if total > fm.upm:
        print(f"⚠ [{master}] asc+|dsc| = {total:.0f} > UPM {fm.upm:.0f}")
    else:
        print(f"✓ [{master}] asc+|dsc| = {total:.0f} (fits within UPM)")
```

fontlab.FontMetrics.ascender.reference: The ascender line position above the baseline (positive value). Typically the height of tall lowercase letters like 'd', 'h', 'l'. In a 1000 UPM font, commonly around 700–800.

fontlab.FontMetrics.capsHeight.reference: The cap height — the top of uppercase letters like 'H', 'I'. Usually slightly below the ascender. In a 1000 UPM font, commonly around 620–720.

fontlab.FontMetrics.descender.reference: The descender line position below the baseline (negative value). This is the lowest point of letters like 'g', 'p', 'y'. In a 1000 UPM font, commonly around -200 to -300.

fontlab.FontMetrics.init.reference: Resets all values to their defaults (0 for all except UPM which becomes 1000).

fontlab.FontMetrics.lineGap.reference: Extra vertical space added between lines when text is laid out at 100% leading. Most text fonts set this to 0, leaving the application to control line spacing. Display fonts sometimes use a non-zero value to suggest minimum spacing.

fontlab.FontMetrics.upm.reference: Units per em — the fundamental scale of the font grid. Most professional fonts use 1000 UPM. A larger UPM (e.g. 2048 for TrueType) allows more precise positioning but is otherwise equivalent.

fontlab.FontMetrics.xHeight.reference: The x-height — the top of the lowercase letters like 'x', 'n', 'o'. A major design parameter that affects the perceived size and readability of the typeface. In a 1000 UPM font, commonly around 450–550.

fontlab.GlyphComponent.reference:
A component reference inside a composite glyph.

## What is GlyphComponent?

A **composite glyph** is a glyph whose shapes are built entirely from references to other glyphs, rather than containing its own outlines. For example, the "é" (e-acute) glyph in most fonts does not contain its own curves — instead, it contains two component references: one to the "e" base glyph and one to "acutecomb" (the combining acute accent).

Each of those references is a `GlyphComponent`. It identifies the base glyph (by name or ID), specifies where to place it (through a transform matrix), and optionally says whether to use anchor-to-anchor alignment instead of a fixed transform.

`GlyphComponent` is the data object describing the reference. On the canvas, each component appears as an `flShape` with `isComponent == True`, and `shape.component` gives you the `GlyphComponent` data.

## Tutorial

```python
from PythonQt.QtGui import QTransform
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import GlyphComponent

font = fl.CurrentFont()

# ============================================================
# Find all composite glyphs in the font and list their
# component references. A composite is a glyph that has no
# direct contours but contains component shapes.
# ============================================================

print("--- Composite Glyphs ---")
composite_count = 0

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    layer = glyph.layers[0]
    components_in_glyph = []

    for shape in layer.shapes:
        if shape.isComponent:
            comp = shape.component
            if comp:
                # Resolve the component's base glyph name:
                try:
                    base_glyph = font.glyph(comp.name_id)
                    base_name  = base_glyph.name if base_glyph else f"id={comp.name_id}"
                except Exception:
                    base_name = f"id={comp.name_id}"

                components_in_glyph.append(
                    f"'{base_name}' "
                    f"(anchors={comp.use_anchors}  "
                    f"width_scale={comp.width_scale:.2f})"
                )

    if components_in_glyph:
        composite_count += 1
        print(f"  '{glyph.name}': {' + '.join(components_in_glyph)}")

print(f"\nTotal composite glyphs: {composite_count}")

# ============================================================
# Inspect the transform of a specific component.
# For composites that use transforms (not anchors), the
# translation tells you where the component was placed.
# ============================================================

if 'eacute' in [g.name for g in font.glyphs]:
    glyph = font['eacute']
    layer = glyph.layers[0]
    for shape in layer.shapes:
        if shape.isComponent:
            comp = shape.component
            tx   = comp.transform
            dx   = tx.dx()   # horizontal translation
            dy   = tx.dy()   # vertical translation
            print(f"\n'eacute' component transform: dx={dx:.0f}  dy={dy:.0f}")
            print(f"  use_anchors: {comp.use_anchors}")

# ============================================================
# Create a GlyphComponent manually.
# This shows what fields you would set to build a composite
# from scratch in a script.
# ============================================================

# Component referencing "e" by name:
comp_e = GlyphComponent("e")
comp_e.use_anchors = False
comp_e.transform   = QTransform()   # identity (no offset)

# Component referencing "acutecomb" placed 300 units above baseline:
comp_acute = GlyphComponent("acutecomb")
comp_acute.use_anchors = True   # let the anchor system position it
comp_acute.transform   = QTransform().translate(0, 300)

print("\nManual component created:")
print(f"  'e' component: use_anchors={comp_e.use_anchors}")
print(f"  'acutecomb' component: use_anchors={comp_acute.use_anchors}")
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Count composites and simple glyphs

```python
import fontlab as fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
composites = 0
simple     = 0

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    layer = glyph.layers[0]
    is_composite = any(s.isComponent for s in layer.shapes)
    if is_composite:
        composites += 1
    elif layer.shapes:
        simple += 1

print(f"Simple: {simple}  Composites: {composites}  "
      f"Total: {composites + simple}")
```

### Find all composites that use a specific base glyph

```python
import fontlab as fl

font    = fl.CurrentFont()
base    = font['a']   # find all composites referencing 'a'
base_id = base.id

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    layer = glyph.layers[0]
    for shape in layer.shapes:
        if shape.isComponent:
            comp = shape.component
            if comp and comp.name_id == base_id:
                print(f"'{glyph.name}' uses '{base.name}' as a component")
```

### Switch all composites from transform-based to anchor-based positioning

```python
import fontlab as fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
for glyph in font.glyphs:
    layer = glyph.layers[0]
    for shape in layer.shapes:
        if shape.isComponent:
            comp = shape.component
            if comp and not comp.use_anchors:
                comp.use_anchors = True

fl.Update()
print("Switched all components to anchor-based positioning.")
```

fontlab.GlyphComponent.name_id.reference: The glyph ID of the base glyph being referenced. Use with `font.glyph(id)` to retrieve the actual `flGlyph`. If you created the component with a name string, `name_id` will be `0` until the component is resolved.

fontlab.GlyphComponent.transform.reference: The 2-D transform applied to the base glyph when it is drawn as part of this composite. A simple translation (e.g. `QTransform().translate(0, 300)`) shifts the component 300 units up. For accented letters with `use_anchors = False`, the translation typically places the accent above the base letter.

fontlab.GlyphComponent.use_anchors.reference: If `True`, the component is positioned by matching its attachment anchor to the base glyph's anchor — for example, the `_top` anchor on the accent snaps to the `top` anchor on the base letter. If `False`, the explicit `transform` is used for positioning. For mark-to-base composites (accented letters), `True` is the standard approach and is required for the font to correctly place diacritics.

fontlab.GlyphComponent.width_scale.reference: Scale factor applied to the component's advance width when compositing. `1.0` uses the base glyph's normal width. Values other than `1.0` are unusual.

fontlab.Info.reference:
Complete font metadata.

## What is Info?

`Info` is the metadata wrapper for all the descriptive information about your font that gets embedded in the file: the family name, style name, designer's name, copyright notice, license, all the OpenType metric values, PostScript hinting parameters, and much more.

It follows the **UFO (Unified Font Object) specification** for attribute names, which means the property names like `openTypeNameDesigner`, `openTypeOS2WeightClass`, and `postscriptFontName` correspond directly to documented UFO 3 attributes. If you know UFO, you already know this interface.

Access `Info` through `package.info` on an `flPackage` wrapper:

```python
package = fl.flPackage(fl.CurrentFont())
info = package.info
print(info.familyName)
info.copyright = "© 2026 My Foundry"
```

All properties read/write the font's metadata storage directly. There is no need to call a save method — changes take effect immediately in the in-memory font.

## Basic Font Identification

These are the most important fields for most type designers.

| Name | Type | Description | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| `familyName` | `string` | The primary family name shown in application font menus (e.g. "Helvetica", "Times New Roman"). All styles in the family should share this name. | read/write |
| `styleName` | `string` | The style name within the family (e.g. "Regular", "Bold Italic", "Condensed Light"). | read/write |
| `styleMapFamilyName` | `string` | The "linked family" name used for bold/italic style mapping in older applications. Applications that only understand the 4-style model (Regular/Bold/Italic/BoldItalic) use this to group styles. | read/write |
| `styleMapStyleName` | `string` | The style position within the linked family group. Must be one of exactly four values: `"regular"`, `"italic"`, `"bold"`, or `"bold italic"`. | read/write |
| `copyright` | `string` | The full copyright statement embedded in the font file (e.g. "Copyright 2026 My Foundry. All rights reserved."). | read/write |
| `trademark` | `string` | The trademark statement, if any. | read/write |
| `note` | `string` | Arbitrary free-text note about the font. Not shown to end users; used for internal documentation. | read/write |
| `unitsPerEm` | `int/float` | Units per em — the scale of the design grid. | read/write |
| `descender` | `int/float` | The descender value for this font's default UPM-relative metrics. | read/write |
| `ascender` | `int/float` | The ascender value. | read/write |
| `xHeight` | `int/float` | The x-height value. | read/write |
| `capHeight` | `int/float` | The cap height value. | read/write |
| `italicAngle` | `int/float` | The italic angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from vertical. `0` for upright fonts; typically `-12` to `-15` for italic. | read/write |
| `versionMajor` | `int` | The major version number of the font (e.g. the `1` in version `1.012`). | read/write |
| `versionMinor` | `int` | The minor version number. | read/write |
| `year` | `int` | Year of creation. Deprecated in UFO 3 in favour of `openTypeHeadCreated`, but still supported. | read/write |
| `panose` | `string` | Legacy PANOSE classification — 10 space-separated numbers. Most modern workflows ignore PANOSE, but it is required for some font delivery platforms. | read/write |

## OpenType hhea Table

The `hhea` (horizontal header) table is used by older applications for line spacing. Values are in design units.

| Name | Type | Description | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| `openTypeHheaAscender` | `int` | The ascender value written to `hhea`. May differ from the design ascender. | read/write |
| `openTypeHheaDescender` | `int` | The descender (negative) written to `hhea`. | read/write |
| `openTypeHheaLineGap` | `int` | Extra vertical space added between lines for `hhea`-based layout. | read/write |
| `openTypeHheaCaretSlopeRise` | `int` | For italic fonts: the rise component of the caret slope vector. | read/write |
| `openTypeHheaCaretSlopeRun` | `int` | For italic fonts: the run component of the caret slope vector. | read/write |
| `openTypeHheaCaretOffset` | `int` | Offset for the text insertion caret in italic fonts. | read/write |

## OpenType OS/2 Table

The OS/2 table carries the most commonly queried font metadata, including the weight class (100–900) that determines how a font appears in application weight lists.

| Name | Type | Description | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| `openTypeOS2WeightClass` | `int` | The weight class: 100=Thin, 200=ExtraLight, 300=Light, 400=Regular, 500=Medium, 600=SemiBold, 700=Bold, 800=ExtraBold, 900=Black. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2WidthClass` | `int` | The width class: 1=UltraCondensed, 2=ExtraCondensed, 3=Condensed, 4=SemiCondensed, 5=Normal, 6=SemiExpanded, 7=Expanded, 8=ExtraExpanded, 9=UltraExpanded. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2WinAscent` | `int` | The Windows-specific ascender (always positive). Controls the clipping boundary in Windows GDI rendering. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2WinDescent` | `int` | The Windows-specific descender (always positive, despite being below baseline). | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2TypoAscender` | `int` | The typographic ascender (for cross-platform line spacing). | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2TypoDescender` | `int` | The typographic descender (negative). | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2TypoLineGap` | `int` | The typographic line gap. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2VendorID` | `string` | Four-character vendor/foundry code registered with Microsoft (e.g. `"ADBO"` for Adobe). | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2Panose` | `list` | OS/2 Panose classification: a list of 10 integers. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2FamilyClass` | `list` | Font family class: `[classID, subclassID]` from the OS/2 specification. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2UnicodeRanges` | `list` | List of bit indices indicating which Unicode ranges the font supports. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2CodePageRanges` | `list` | List of bit indices indicating which Windows code pages the font supports. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2StrikeoutSize` | `int` | Thickness of the strikethrough stroke in design units. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2StrikeoutPosition` | `int` | Vertical position of the strikethrough (from baseline). | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2Type` | `list` | Embedding permission flags (`fsType`). | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2Selection` | `list` | Style selection flags (`fsSelection`) — bold, italic, regular, etc. Do not include bits 0, 5, or 6. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2SubscriptXSize` | `int` | Suggested subscript glyph width. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2SubscriptYSize` | `int` | Suggested subscript glyph height. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2SubscriptXOffset` | `int` | Suggested subscript horizontal offset. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2SubscriptYOffset` | `int` | Suggested subscript vertical offset (downward). | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2SuperscriptXSize` | `int` | Suggested superscript width. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2SuperscriptYSize` | `int` | Suggested superscript height. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2SuperscriptXOffset` | `int` | Suggested superscript horizontal offset. | read/write |
| `openTypeOS2SuperscriptYOffset` | `int` | Suggested superscript vertical offset (upward). | read/write |

| Name | Type | Description | Access |

## PostScript / CFF

These are the PostScript-specific font-level metadata fields.

| Name | Type | Description | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| `postscriptFontName` | `string` | The PostScript font name (the `FontName` in a Type 1 dictionary). Should be short, no spaces, no special characters. | read/write |
| `postscriptFullName` | `string` | The PostScript full name (`FullName` in the font dictionary). | read/write |
| `postscriptWeightName` | `string` | The PostScript weight string (e.g. `"Regular"`, `"Bold"`). | read/write |
| `postscriptUniqueID` | `int` | PostScript unique ID number. | read/write |
| `postscriptIsFixedPitch` | `bool` | `True` if the font is monospaced — all glyphs have the same advance width. | read/write |
| `postscriptForceBold` | `bool` | The ForceBold flag in the CFF Private dictionary. | read/write |
| `postscriptDefaultWidthX` | `int/float` | Default advance width for glyphs. Used to save space in the CFF data when most glyphs share one width. | read/write |
| `postscriptNominalWidthX` | `int/float` | The "nominal" width deviation stored in CFF. | read/write |
| `postscriptBlueValues` | `list` | Up to 14 blue zone values (in pairs). These define the horizontal bands used for PS alignment-zone hinting. Example: `[0, 10, 490, 500, 690, 700]` for baseline+overshoot, x-height+overshoot, capHeight+overshoot. | read/write |
| `postscriptOtherBlues` | `list` | Up to 10 "other blues" values — the downward-facing alignment zones (for the descender area). | read/write |
| `postscriptFamilyBlues` | `list` | Family-level blue values, shared across all styles to ensure consistent zone snapping. | read/write |
| `postscriptFamilyOtherBlues` | `list` | Family-level other blues. | read/write |
| `postscriptStemSnapH` | `list` | Up to 12 representative horizontal stem widths. These are the widths of horizontal strokes in the font (e.g. the thickness of the crossbar on 'H'). | read/write |
| `postscriptStemSnapV` | `list` | Up to 12 representative vertical stem widths — the thickness of vertical strokes (e.g. the left stroke of 'H'). | read/write |
| `postscriptBlueFuzz` | `int/float` | How much to extend each blue zone. | read/write |
| `postscriptBlueScale` | `float` | PPEM at which overshoots stop being suppressed. | read/write |
| `postscriptBlueShift` | `int/float` | Minimum overshoot for suppression. | read/write |
| `postscriptUnderlinePosition` | `int/float` | Vertical position of the underline (from baseline, negative values go below). | read/write |
| `postscriptUnderlineThickness` | `int/float` | Thickness of the underline stroke. | read/write |
| `postscriptDefaultCharacter` | `string` | Name of the glyph used as the default character in Windows PFM metrics. | read/write |
| `postscriptWindowsCharacterSet` | `int` | Windows character set identifier for this font. | read/write |

```python
    "copyright":                info.copyright,
    "openTypeNameDesigner":     info.openTypeNameDesigner,
    "openTypeNameManufacturer": info.openTypeNameManufacturer,
    "openTypeNameLicense":      info.openTypeNameLicense,
    "postscriptFontName":       info.postscriptFontName,
    "openTypeOS2VendorID":      info.openTypeOS2VendorID,
}

print("--- Required fields check ---")
all_ok = True
for field, value in required.items():
    status = "✓" if value else "✗ MISSING"
    if not value:
        all_ok = False
    print(f"  {status}  {field}: '{value or ''}'")

if all_ok:
    print("\nAll required fields are filled.")
else:
    print("\nSome fields are missing — fill them before export.")
```

### Custom Unicode–name mapping and Other settings

| Property | Type | Access | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nametablePath` | str or None | read/write | Font-wide custom `.nam` path; assignment reloads the mapping. Empty/None selects the standard mapping. |
| `otherData` | dict | read/write | Snapshot of additional settings; assign a dictionary to patch selected entries. |

`font.info.nametablePath` reads or sets the font-wide `.nam` path shown in
Font Info > Other. Assignment reloads the mapping immediately. Use `""` or
`None` to restore the standard mapping. Relative paths resolve from the font's
folder; an unreadable file retains its configured path and uses standard mapping
with a warning.

`font.info.otherData` returns a dictionary snapshot of the current master's
Other settings (including loop resolution and TrueType hinting controls), plus
the font-wide `nametablePath`. Assign a dictionary to patch selected entries;
mutating the returned snapshot alone does not update the font. PANOSE retains
its existing `font.info.panose` / `font.info.openTypeOS2Panose` access.

```python
font.info.nametablePath = "names/custom.nam"
font.info.otherData = {"nametablePath": "names/custom.nam"}
font.info.otherData = {"nametablePath": None}  # standard mapping
```

MCP uses `set_font_info` with
`{"font_info": {"other_data": {"nametablePath": "names/custom.nam"}}}`.
`otherData` is also accepted. `get_font_info` returns the configured value in
`other_data.nametablePath`. This setting applies to every master; do not put it
inside `masters[]`.

fontlab.Interval.reference:
A parametric range on a contour.

## What is Interval?

Imagine "selecting" a portion of a contour — not a node, but a stretch of curve from 25% to 75% of the way along the path. An `Interval` stores exactly that: two parametric values `t0` and `t1` defining a sub-range of a Bézier contour.

Intervals are used internally by the node selection system, by split-curve operations, and by any tool that needs to work with a portion of a contour rather than whole segments. You will mostly encounter them when writing custom canvas tools that deal with selecting or cutting parts of curves.

## Tutorial

```python
from fontlab import Interval

# ============================================================
# Create an interval covering the middle third of a contour.
# This represents parametric positions 33.3% to 66.7% along
# the contour arc.
# ============================================================

iv = Interval()
iv.setT0T1(0.333, 0.667)

print(f"Interval: t0={iv.t0:.3f}  t1={iv.t1:.3f}")
print(f"Length:   {iv.d:.3f}")
print(f"Midpoint: {iv.middle():.3f}")
print(f"Is empty: {iv.isEmpty()}")

# ============================================================
# Map a relative position within the interval to an
# absolute contour position.
# "Where is the 1/4 point of this interval on the contour?"
# ============================================================

# 0.25 = 1/4 of the way through [0.333, 0.667]
quarter_abs = iv.toAbsolute(0.25)
print(f"\n1/4 through interval → absolute t = {quarter_abs:.3f}")
# Expected: 0.333 + 0.25 * (0.667 - 0.333) = ~0.417

# Map back: given absolute t=0.5, where is that in the interval?
fraction = iv.toInterval(0.5)
print(f"Absolute t=0.5 → interval fraction = {fraction:.3f}")
# Expected: (0.5 - 0.333) / (0.667 - 0.333) = ~0.5

# ============================================================
# Reverse the interval — same coverage, opposite direction.
# Useful when you need to iterate a selection in reverse.
# ============================================================

rev = iv.reversed()
print(f"\nReversed: t0={rev.t0:.3f}  t1={rev.t1:.3f}")

# ============================================================
# An empty interval — covers nothing.
# This is what you get when a hit test lands exactly on a node.
# ============================================================

empty_iv = Interval()
empty_iv.setT0T1(0.5, 0.5)
print(f"\nEmpty interval: isEmpty={empty_iv.isEmpty()}  d={empty_iv.d}")
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Check whether a parametric position falls within an interval

```python
from fontlab import Interval

iv = Interval()
iv.setT0T1(0.2, 0.8)

def contains(interval, t):
    return interval.t0 <= t <= interval.t1

print(contains(iv, 0.5))   # True
print(contains(iv, 0.1))   # False
```

### Split an interval into equal thirds

```python
from fontlab import Interval

iv = Interval()
iv.setT0T1(0.0, 1.0)

third = iv.d / 3.0
parts = []
for i in range(3):
    part = Interval()
    part.setT0T1(iv.t0 + i * third, iv.t0 + (i + 1) * third)
    parts.append(part)
    print(f"Part {i}: [{part.t0:.3f}, {part.t1:.3f}]")
```

fontlab.Interval.d.reference: The length of the interval: `t1 - t0`. A convenient way to check how much of the contour is covered by this interval.

fontlab.Interval.isEmpty.reference: Returns `True` if `t0 == t1` (a zero-length interval that covers no curve area). An empty interval typically results from querying a point that lands exactly on a node.

fontlab.Interval.key.reference: An integer hash code that uniquely identifies this `(t0, t1)` pair. Used internally for caching interval-based computations.

fontlab.Interval.middle.reference: Returns the midpoint of the interval: `(t0 + t1) / 2`. A quick way to find the centre of the selected stretch of curve.

fontlab.Interval.reversed.reference: Returns a new interval with `t0` and `t1` swapped. The reversed interval covers the same portion of the contour but in the opposite traversal direction. Useful when iterating a selection backwards.

fontlab.Interval.setT0T1.reference: Sets both `t0` and `t1` simultaneously. Preferred over setting them one at a time to avoid momentarily invalid states where `t0 > t1`.

fontlab.Interval.t0.reference: The start of the interval. `0.0` means the very beginning of the contour arc.

fontlab.Interval.t1.reference: The end of the interval. The interpretation depends on whether you are using per-segment parametrisation (0..1 per segment) or full-contour parametrisation.

fontlab.Interval.toAbsolute.reference: Converts a value `v` expressed as a fraction of this interval (0 = start, 1 = end) to an absolute parametric value on the contour. For example, if the interval is [0.25, 0.75], then `toAbsolute(0.5)` returns `0.5` (the midpoint of the full contour).

fontlab.Interval.toInterval.reference: The inverse of `toAbsolute`. Converts an absolute parametric value `absv` to a 0..1 fraction relative to this interval. Useful when you have a global contour position and want to know where it falls within a given interval.

fontlab.LocationValue.reference:
## What is a LocationValue?

A `LocationValue` is the value stored for a single axis in an `flLocation`. For the vast majority of uses, a `LocationValue` is just a number — you set it to `400` and read it back as `400`. But it can also be **anisotropic**, which means it carries two slightly different numbers.

### Isotropic vs anisotropic

**Isotropic** (the normal case): a single number. Both sides of the default on the axis use the same value. When you write `loc["wght"] = 700`, you're creating an isotropic `LocationValue` with `x == y == 700`.

**Anisotropic**: two numbers, `x` and `y`. These represent the value on the *approach* side (coming from the default toward the minimum) and the *departure* side (going from the default toward the maximum). This is used for rare cases like optical-size axes where the interpolation behavior at the default point is asymmetric — the letter shapes transition differently when you go up vs. down from the default.

In practice, you'll almost always use isotropic values. Anisotropic values are a niche feature.

```python
# Isotropic (normal):
v = LocationValue(400)
print(float(v))             # 400.0

# Anisotropic (rare, advanced):
v2 = LocationValue(400, 450)
# x=400 on one side of the default, y=450 on the other
```

When `x == y`, a `LocationValue` displays and accepts as a plain number. When `x != y`, it appears as a `(x, y)` tuple.

## Tutorial

```python
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import flLocation, LocationValue

font = fl.CurrentFont()

# ============================================================
# 1. Creating a location from scratch
# ============================================================
# The simplest approach: start with an empty location, then
# add axis values one by one, just like filling a dictionary.

loc = flLocation()
loc["wght"] = 400      # Weight axis at Regular (400)
loc["wdth"] = 100      # Width axis at Normal (100)

print("My location:", dict(loc))   # {'wght': 400.0, 'wdth': 100.0}

# ============================================================
# 2. Creating a location from a dict (most convenient)
# ============================================================
# You can pass a plain Python dict directly to the constructor.
# This is the cleanest way to build a location in one line.

bold_loc = flLocation({"wght": 700, "wdth": 100})
condensed_loc = flLocation({"wght": 400, "wdth": 75})
bold_condensed = flLocation({"wght": 700, "wdth": 75})

print("Bold location:", dict(bold_loc))

# ============================================================
# 3. Reading values from a location
# ============================================================
# Use the axis tag as the key, just like a dictionary.
# The value comes back as a LocationValue, but it acts like a number.

wght_val = bold_loc["wght"]
print(f"Weight: {wght_val}")          # prints: 700 (or similar)
print(f"As float: {float(wght_val)}")  # explicitly convert to float

# ============================================================
# 4. Updating values in a location
# ============================================================

loc["wght"] = 600      # change weight to Semibold
print("Updated weight:", float(loc["wght"]))   # 600.0

# ============================================================
# 5. Checking what axes are in a location
# ============================================================

print("Axes in location:", list(loc.keys()))
print("Has wght?", "wght" in loc)
print("Has opsz?", "opsz" in loc)   # False if optical size not set
print("Number of axes:", len(loc))

# ============================================================
# 6. Iterating over a location
# ============================================================
# Iterate just like a dict — you get the axis tags, and then
# look up each value.

print("All axis values:")
for tag in loc:
    print(f"  {tag} = {float(loc[tag]):.0f}")

# Or iterate over .items() for tag+value pairs:
for tag, val in loc.items():
    print(f"  {tag} → {float(val):.1f}")

# ============================================================
# 7. Removing an axis from a location
# ============================================================
# If you want a location that only specifies some axes,
# you can remove others with del.

loc2 = flLocation({"wght": 300, "wdth": 75, "ital": 0})
del loc2["ital"]                        # remove the italic axis
print("After removing ital:", list(loc2.keys()))   # ["wght", "wdth"]

# ============================================================
# 8. LocationValue — isotropic vs anisotropic
# ============================================================
# Normally you'll just use plain numbers. But here's how
# LocationValue works if you need to inspect it directly.

# Isotropic (the everyday case):
v_iso = LocationValue(400)
print("Isotropic value:", float(v_iso))   # 400.0

# Anisotropic (rare — for axes with asymmetric interpolation):
v_aniso = LocationValue(400, 450)
# Use this in a location:
loc["opsz"] = v_aniso

# ============================================================
# 9. Reading the current design-space location
# ============================================================
# font.currentLocation() tells you which location the font
# editor is currently showing. This is useful if you want to
# run a script that operates on "wherever the designer is right now."

cur_loc = font.currentLocation()
print("\nCurrently viewing:")
for tag in cur_loc:
    print(f"  {tag} = {float(cur_loc[tag]):.0f}")

# ============================================================
# 10. Reading instance locations
# ============================================================
# Each named instance has a location that defines exactly where
# it lives in design space. You can read and compare these.

print("\nAll named instances:")
for inst in font.instances:
    loc_parts = [
        f"{tag}={float(inst.location[tag]):.0f}"
        for tag in inst.location
    ]
    print(f"  '{inst.name}': {', '.join(loc_parts)}")

# ============================================================
# 11. Building a location to navigate to a specific master
# ============================================================
# Use setCurrentLocation to move the editor view to a specific
# point in design space. This is equivalent to dragging the
# axis sliders in the Variations panel.

# Navigate to Bold:
# font.setCurrentLocation(bold_loc)

# Navigate to Condensed:
# font.setCurrentLocation(condensed_loc)

# ============================================================
# 12. Converting a location to a plain Python dict
# ============================================================
# Sometimes you need a plain dict — for JSON export, for printing,
# or to pass to code that doesn't know about flLocation.

plain_dict = {tag: float(loc[tag]) for tag in loc}
print("As plain dict:", plain_dict)

fl.Update()
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Find the instance closest to the current location

```python
# Useful when you want to know which named preset the user
# is currently looking at, even if they've dragged a slider away.
import fontlab as fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
cur = font.currentLocation()

def location_distance(loc_a, loc_b):
    """Simple Euclidean distance between two locations in design space."""
    total = 0.0
    for tag in loc_a:
        if tag in loc_b:
            diff = float(loc_a[tag]) - float(loc_b[tag])
            total += diff * diff
    return total ** 0.5

closest = min(font.instances,
              key=lambda inst: location_distance(cur, inst.location))
print(f"Closest instance to current view: '{closest.name}'")
```

### Build a location from a dict of axis names (not tags)

```python
# If you have axis names ("Weight") rather than tags ("wght"),
# this helper converts them for you.
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import flLocation

font = fl.CurrentFont()
axes_by_name = {a.name: a for a in font.axes}

def location_from_names(name_dict):
    """Build an flLocation from a dict keyed by axis name."""
    loc = flLocation()
    for axis_name, value in name_dict.items():
        if axis_name in axes_by_name:
            loc[axes_by_name[axis_name].tag] = value
    return loc

loc = location_from_names({"Weight": 700, "Width": 75})
print("Built location:", {k: float(v) for k, v in loc.items()})
```

### Print all axis values as normalized numbers

```python
# Show what each instance looks like in the OpenType
# normalized range (−1, 0, 1 scale).
import fontlab as fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
axes_by_tag = {a.tag: a for a in font.axes}

for inst in font.instances:
    normals = {}
    for tag, val in inst.location.items():
        if tag in axes_by_tag:
            normals[tag] = round(axes_by_tag[tag].normalize(float(val)), 3)
    print(f"'{inst.name}': {normals}")
```

### Check whether two locations are identical

```python
# Compare two locations to see if they point to the same place.
from fontlab import flLocation

def locations_equal(a, b, tolerance=0.01):
    if set(a.keys()) != set(b.keys()):
        return False
    return all(
        abs(float(a[tag]) - float(b[tag])) < tolerance
        for tag in a
    )

loc1 = flLocation({"wght": 700, "wdth": 100})
loc2 = flLocation({"wght": 700, "wdth": 100})
loc3 = flLocation({"wght": 700, "wdth": 75})

print(locations_equal(loc1, loc2))   # True
print(locations_equal(loc1, loc3))   # False
```

### Walk all instances and print whether they're at an axis edge

```python
# Identify which instances are at the min or max of any axis.
# These are your "extreme" corner masters.
import fontlab as fl

font = fl.CurrentFont()
axes_by_tag = {a.tag: a for a in font.axes}

for inst in font.instances:
    edges = []
    for tag, val in inst.location.items():
        if tag in axes_by_tag:
            if axes_by_tag[tag].onEdge(float(val)):
                edges.append(tag)
    if edges:
        print(f"'{inst.name}' is on the edge of: {edges}")
    else:
        print(f"'{inst.name}' is in the interior of design space")
```

### Create a grid of instances for a two-axis font

```python
# Automatically create instances at every combination of
# axis stops in a two-axis Weight × Width font.
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import flInstance, flLocation

font = fl.CurrentFont()

weight_stops = [300, 400, 600, 700]   # Light, Regular, Semibold, Bold
width_stops  = [75, 100, 125]         # Condensed, Normal, Extended

weight_names = {300: "Light", 400: "Regular", 600: "Semibold", 700: "Bold"}
width_names  = {75: "Condensed", 100: "", 125: "Extended"}

for wght in weight_stops:
    for wdth in width_stops:
        inst = flInstance()
        # Combine weight + width name, strip extra spaces
        parts = [weight_names[wght], width_names[wdth]]
        inst.name = " ".join(p for p in parts if p)
        inst.exportable = True

        loc = flLocation()
        loc["wght"] = wght
        loc["wdth"] = wdth
        inst.location = loc

        font.addInstance(inst)
        print(f"Added: '{inst.name}'  wght={wght} wdth={wdth}")

fl.Update()
```

fontlab.PaintBrush.reference:
Brush settings for drawing tools.

## What is PaintBrush?

The `PaintBrush` defines the shape of the brush used by FontLab's scribble and colour-font drawing tools. It controls how thick the brush stroke is, whether it is circular or elliptical, and at what angle. You can script brush settings to create consistent stroke effects programmatically.

## Tutorial

```python
from fontlab import PaintBrush

# A calligraphic-style brush at 45 degrees:
brush = PaintBrush()
brush.init()
brush.size     = 40.0
brush.flatness = 0.2      # very flat, like a broad-nib pen
brush.angle    = 45.0     # classic calligraphic angle
brush.render(1.0)

print(f"Brush: {brush.toString()}")

# A round brush:
round_brush = PaintBrush()
round_brush.init()
round_brush.size = 20.0
round_brush.flatness = 1.0
round_brush.angle = 0.0
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Set up a calligraphic brush

```python
from fontlab import PaintBrush

brush = PaintBrush()
brush.init()
brush.size     = 60.0    # overall diameter in glyph units
brush.flatness = 0.15    # very flat → calligraphic nib effect
brush.angle    = 30.0    # nib rotation angle in degrees
print(f"Brush: size={brush.size}  flatness={brush.flatness}  angle={brush.angle}°")
print(brush.toString())
```

### Apply a brush to the workspace

```python
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import PaintBrush

ws = fl.flWorkspace.instance()
brush = PaintBrush()
brush.init()
brush.size     = 40.0
brush.flatness = 0.2
brush.angle    = 15.0
ws.paintBrush = brush
fl.Update()
print("Brush applied to workspace.")
```

fontlab.PaintBrush.angle.reference: The rotation angle of the brush in degrees. `0` = upright. Set to `45` for a classic calligraphic angle.

fontlab.PaintBrush.assign.reference: Copies all properties from another `PaintBrush` into this one. Use this to clone a brush configuration.

fontlab.PaintBrush.flatness.reference: The aspect ratio of the brush. `1.0` = circular. Values less than `1.0` produce an elliptical (flat) brush — good for a calligraphic chisel effect.

fontlab.PaintBrush.init.reference: Resets the brush to its default settings: size 50, flatness 0.5, angle 30 degrees.

fontlab.PaintBrush.render.reference: Pre-renders the brush outline at the given canvas zoom `scale`. Must be called after changing brush properties before the brush is drawn on screen.

fontlab.PaintBrush.shape.reference: The custom PaintBrushShape profile value. This is not an enum of brush names.

fontlab.PaintBrush.size.reference: The brush diameter in glyph units. Larger values produce thicker strokes.

fontlab.PaintBrush.toString.reference: Returns a string representation of the brush settings. Can be stored in preferences or written to a JSON file for later recall.

fontlab.PaintBrushShape.reference:
The custom brush profile stored in `PaintBrush.shape`. This is a data object, not an enum of brush names.

`PaintBrushShape()` uses the native brush-profile defaults. Positional fields follow the table order; field keywords are supported. `asTuple()` and `asDict()` provide snapshots; indexing, item assignment and `len()` follow the same order. Modify an existing profile read from a PaintBrush, then assign it back to `brush.shape` and render the brush again.

fontlab.PaintBrushShape.data.reference: Brush-profile samples, converted through the native sequence converter.

A value wrapper for a font's Smart Corners settings. Read it from `flPackage.smartCornerParameters`, modify the copy, and assign it back to apply the settings.

## Construction and fields

`SmartCornerParameters()` uses native defaults: `curvature=0.67`, `inktrap_len=2.0`. Positional fields follow that order; keyword field initialization is also supported, for example `SmartCornerParameters(curvature=0.7, inktrap_len=3.0)`.

| `inktrap_len` | float | read/write | Native ink-trap length parameter. |

`asTuple()` returns the fields in constructor order; `asDict()` returns a dictionary snapshot. The wrapper supports indexing, item assignment and `len()`. Editing a snapshot does not update the font until it is assigned back. Direct model edits still need the usual history and change notifications.

fontlab.TransformFrame.reference:
Interactive Bounding Frame.

## What is TransformFrame?

The `TransformFrame` is the rectangular selection bounding box you see in FontLab when you choose the Transform tool and select objects. It has eight handles (four corners plus four mid-edge points) that you can drag to scale, rotate, slant, or reflect the selected content. The box can be freely rotated, so it is not always axis-aligned.

In scripts, `TransformFrame` lets you compute what transform to apply based on dragging one handle to a new position — essentially implementing the math behind FontLab's Transform tool in your own scripts. You build a frame, manipulate it, then call `getTransform()` to get the resulting `QTransform` that you apply to the actual geometry.

## Handle Query Methods

| Signature | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `QPointF mt()` | Returns the **mid-top** handle position — the midpoint of the top edge. |
| `QPointF mb()` | Returns the **mid-bottom** handle position — the midpoint of the bottom edge. |
| `QPointF ml()` | Returns the **mid-left** handle position. |
| `QPointF mr()` | Returns the **mid-right** handle position. |
| `QPolygonF polygon()` | Returns the frame as a four-point polygon (the four corners in order: TL, TR, BR, BL). |
| `double lh()` | The height of the left side of the frame (distance from `bl` to `tl`). |
| `double mh()` | The average height: `(lh() + rh()) / 2`. Useful when the frame is slightly non-rectangular due to floating-point rounding. |
| `double rh()` | The height of the right side of the frame (distance from `br` to `tr`). |
| `double tw()` | The width of the top edge (distance from `tl` to `tr`). |
| `double mw()` | The average width: `(tw() + bw()) / 2`. |
| `double bw()` | The width of the bottom edge (distance from `bl` to `br`). |
| `QRectF boundingRect()` | Returns the axis-aligned bounding rectangle that fully contains the (possibly rotated) frame. |

## Transformation Methods

| Signature | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `TransformFrame getMapped(QTransform t)` | Returns a new `TransformFrame` with all four corners mapped through the transform `t`. Use this to preview what the frame will look like after a transformation, without modifying the original frame. |
| `QPointF getControlPos(TransformFrameControls)` | Returns the current canvas position of one of the eight control handles. Pass a `TransformFrameControls` enum value: `TL`, `TR`, `BL`, `BR`, `MT`, `MB`, `ML`, or `MR`. |
| `void translate(QPointF)` | Moves the entire frame by the given offset vector. All four corners are shifted by the same amount. |
| `void rotate(double)` | Rotates the frame by the given angle in **degrees**, counter-clockwise. The frame rotates around its centre point `cr`. |
| `void scale(QPointF s)` | Scales the frame: `s.x()` is the horizontal scale factor, `s.y()` is the vertical. Values greater than 1 enlarge; values less than 1 shrink. Scaling is relative to the frame's centre. |
| `void slant(double angle, double angle)` | Applies an oblique (slant) transform using the given horizontal and vertical angle values. This is what the Slant action uses internally. |
| `void horizontalReflection()` | Mirrors the frame horizontally: left becomes right, right becomes left. The centre stays fixed. |
| `void verticalReflection()` | Mirrors the frame vertically: top becomes bottom. The centre stays fixed. |
| `void flipHorizontal()` | Flips the frame horizontally (same effect as `horizontalReflection`). |
| `void flipVertical()` | Flips the frame vertically (same as `verticalReflection`). |
| `void rotate180()` | Rotates the frame exactly 180 degrees. Equivalent to both a horizontal and a vertical flip. |
| `void initCenter()` | Recomputes the centre point `cr` from the current corner positions. Always call this after manually repositioning corners so that rotations and scales pivot correctly. |
| `void doTransformation(int code, QPointF value)` | Applies a transformation identified by `code` (a `TransformFrameControls` integer) by the delta `value`. This is the core method behind drag-to-transform interactions — it is what gets called when you drag a handle in the editor. |
| `QTransform getTransform()` | Returns the net `QTransform` that maps the original (pre-interaction) frame to its current state. Apply this transform to the selected objects to commit the change to the geometry. |
| `void prepareTransformations([TransformFrameControls control, QPointF p,] double scale)` | Prepares the frame for an interactive transformation session. `scale` is the current canvas zoom factor. Optionally constrain to one control point and provide the starting mouse position `p`. |
| `void setControlPos([TransformFrameControls control,] QPointF position, bool reflection, bool proportional, bool fixed)` | Moves a handle to `position`. `reflection` mirrors the change to the opposite handle symmetrically; `proportional` locks the aspect ratio; `fixed` locks the opposite side in place. |
| `void setProjectionPos([TransformFrameControls control,] QPointF position, bool reflection, bool proportional, bool fixed)` | Like `setControlPos` but uses perspective-preserving (projection) mathematics for the handle movement. Used for the Perspective transformation. |

## Corner Properties

| Name | Type | Access | Description |
|------|------|--------|-------------|
| `tl` | `QPointF` | rw | **Top-left** corner of the frame. |
| `tr` | `QPointF` | rw | **Top-right** corner of the frame. |
| `bl` | `QPointF` | rw | **Bottom-left** corner of the frame. |
| `br` | `QPointF` | rw | **Bottom-right** corner of the frame. |
| `cr` | `QPointF` | rw | **Centre** point of the frame. This is the pivot used for rotations and scales. Call `initCenter()` to recompute it from corners. |

## Tutorial

```python
from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import TransformFrame

# ============================================================
# Goal: Scale a shape 2× horizontally using TransformFrame.
#
# The workflow is:
#   1. Get the shape's bounding box
#   2. Build a TransformFrame that matches it
#   3. Apply a transformation to the frame
#   4. Retrieve the resulting QTransform via getTransform()
#   5. Apply that QTransform to the actual shape geometry
# ============================================================

font  = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font['A']
layer = glyph.layers[0]
shape = layer.shapes[0]

bbox = shape.boundingBox    # returns a QRectF in glyph units
print(f"Shape bounding box: {bbox}")

# ============================================================
# Step 1: Build a frame from the bounding box corners.
# We set the four corners manually, then call initCenter()
# so that rotations and scales use the correct pivot point.
# ============================================================

frame = TransformFrame()
frame.tl = QPointF(bbox.left(),  bbox.top())
frame.tr = QPointF(bbox.right(), bbox.top())
frame.bl = QPointF(bbox.left(),  bbox.bottom())
frame.br = QPointF(bbox.right(), bbox.bottom())
frame.initCenter()   # compute centre from corners

print(f"Frame centre: {frame.cr}")
print(f"Frame width:  {frame.mw():.0f}")
print(f"Frame height: {frame.mh():.0f}")

# ============================================================
# Step 2: Scale the frame — 2× wide, same height.
# scale() takes a QPointF where x = horizontal factor,
# y = vertical factor.
# ============================================================

frame.scale(QPointF(2.0, 1.0))
print(f"\nAfter 2× horizontal scale:")
print(f"  New width: {frame.mw():.0f}")

# ============================================================
# Step 3: Get the net transform and apply it to the shape.
# getTransform() returns the QTransform that maps the
# original frame to the current (scaled) frame.
# ============================================================

tx = frame.getTransform()
print(f"Net transform: {tx}")

shape.transformBy(tx)
fl.Update()
print("Done — shape scaled 2× horizontally.")
```

fontlab.YPanelManager.reference:
Dockable panel system.

## What is YPanelManager?

FontLab's sidebar and panel system is managed by `YPanelManager`. Every dockable panel you see in FontLab — the Layers panel, the Glyph panel, the Properties panel — is registered with and managed by this singleton.

If you want to **create a custom side panel** that always appears in the FontLab UI (rather than a separate window), you subclass `YPanelWidget` and register it with `YPanelManager.instance()`.

## Getting the instance

There is always exactly one `YPanelManager` in a running FontLab:

```python
from fontlab import YPanelManager
pm = YPanelManager.instance()
```

## Tutorial

`YPanelManager` lets you open, close, and inspect FontLab's dockable panels. Here is how to work with both the built-in panels and your own custom ones.

```python
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import YPanelManager, YPanelWidget

# ============================================================
# Get the panel manager singleton.
# ============================================================

pm = YPanelManager.instance()

print(f"Registered panels: {len(pm.registeredPanels)}")
for panel in pm.registeredPanels:
    visible = pm.panelVisible(panel)
    status  = "open" if visible else "closed"
    print(f"  [{status}] id={panel.id:3d}  '{panel.title}'")

print(f"\nCurrently open: {len(pm.panels)}")

# ============================================================
# Toggle a panel open/closed by its title.
# ============================================================

target_title = "Layers"   # change to any panel title you see above
target_panel = next(
    (p for p in pm.registeredPanels if p.title == target_title), None
)
if target_panel:
    if pm.panelVisible(target_panel):
        pm.closePanel(target_panel)
        print(f"Closed '{target_title}'")
    else:
        pm.openPanel(target_panel)
        print(f"Opened '{target_title}'")
else:
    print(f"Panel '{target_title}' not found.")

# ============================================================
# Create and register a minimal custom panel.
# (Full UI requires Qt widgets from PyQt5 or PySide2.)
# ============================================================

# class MyInfoPanel(YPanelWidget):
#     def __init__(self):
#         super().__init__()
#         self.title           = "Glyph Info"
#         self.defaultEdge     = 2              # right side
#         self.minimumPanelSize = fl.QSize(200, 150)
#
# panel = MyInfoPanel()
# pm.registerPanel(panel)
# pm.openPanel(panel)
# print(f"Custom panel id={panel.id}")
```

```python
if panel:
```
