fontlab.flObject.clearAboveHistory.reference: Removes all history states above the given index, discarding any redo states beyond that point. Useful when you want to commit a script's changes as the new canonical state and prevent re-doing past the script.

fontlab.flObject.clearFlag.reference: Clears (turns off) flag bit `f`. After this call, `flag(f)` will return `False`. Use this when you want to unmark a specific flag without touching other flags on the same object.

fontlab.flObject.clearFlags.reference: Clears all flag bits on this object at once, regardless of which ones were set. A useful reset between processing passes when you want a clean slate.

fontlab.flObject.clone.reference: Creates a deep copy of this object. The copy is completely independent — it gets a new unique ID and none of your changes to the clone will affect the original. Use this when you want to add a copy of a shape to a different layer without disturbing the source.

fontlab.flObject.cloneObject.reference: Creates a deep copy of the given object and returns it. The clone is fully independent — modifying it will not affect the original. This is the class-level version of the instance method `clone()`.

fontlab.flObject.createObject.reference: Allocates a new object of the given type ID and returns it as a generic `flObject`. The integer argument is the type constant (same system as `.type`). Returns `None` if the type is not recognized. You rarely need this — use the concrete subclass constructors instead.

fontlab.flObject.currentHistoryState.reference: Returns the index of the current history state. Think of this as the "now" pointer in the history timeline. Subtracting 1 and restoring gets you one undo step back.

fontlab.flObject.flag.reference: Returns `True` if bit flag `f` is currently set on this object, `False` otherwise. The argument is a small integer (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) identifying which flag bit to check. You define what each number means in your own scripts.

fontlab.flObject.getProperties.reference: Legacy object-valued property list (`QList<flObject>`); this is not a list of metadata keys and is empty for nodes.

fontlab.flObject.getProperty.reference: Returns the stored QVariant converted to Python, or `None` when absent. Strings and numbers retain their types.

fontlab.flObject.getPropertyFloat.reference: Returns the value stored under the given key as a floating-point number. Saves you from manually calling `float()` on the string result of `getProperty`.

fontlab.flObject.getPropertyInt.reference: Returns the value stored under the given key as an integer. A convenience wrapper that handles the string-to-int conversion automatically.

fontlab.flObject.hasChanges.reference: `True` if this object has unsaved changes that have not yet been written to disk. FontLab uses this to decide whether to show the "save?" prompt when closing.

fontlab.flObject.hasHistoryState.reference: Returns `True` if a history state at the given index exists for this object. Use this before calling `restoreHistoryState` to avoid errors when navigating near the start or end of the history.

fontlab.flObject.hasHistoryStates.reference: `True` if this object has at least one recorded history state. If `False`, there is nothing to undo/redo for this object.

fontlab.flObject.haveObject.reference: Given an object ID (an integer), returns `True` if an object with that ID currently exists in the font model. Useful for validating stored IDs before trying to use them — for example, after undo operations that might have removed an object.

fontlab.flObject.historyStates.reference: Returns a list of history state indices for this object. Pass `True` to get only the committed (accepted) states; pass `False` to include pending/uncommitted states. Useful for understanding how many undo steps are available.

fontlab.flObject.id.reference: The unique integer identifier assigned to this object when it was created. No two live objects in the same session share an ID. Use this to track objects across operations or to look them up later with `haveObject()`.

fontlab.flObject.independedAll.reference: Breaks all dependency links that make this object react to changes in other objects. After calling this, the object stands alone — useful before deleting or repurposing an object that was part of a linked structure.

fontlab.flObject.initialHistoryState.reference: Returns the index of the oldest available history state — in other words, how far back you can undo. This is the floor of the history range.

fontlab.flObject.instanceType.reference: Returns the integer type identifier for this class. Every subclass of `flObject` has a unique type constant — this lets you check "what kind of object is this?" at the class level, before you even have an instance.

fontlab.flObject.isChanged.reference: `True` if this object has been modified since the last explicit `changed()` call was processed. Slightly different from `hasChanges` — this one tracks the in-memory dirty state rather than the disk-save state.

fontlab.flObject.isEqual.reference: Compares this object to another for deep equality. Unlike Python's `==` (which compares references), `isEqual` checks whether the two objects have the same structural content. Two separately constructed shapes with identical contours will return `True`.

fontlab.flObject.isNull.reference: `True` if this object handle points to nothing — the C++ pointer is null. This should not happen in normal use, but can occur if you receive an object from a method that failed silently.

fontlab.flObject.isPresent.reference: `True` if this object is currently part of its parent's collection — for example, a shape that is attached to a layer. When you remove a shape from a layer, `isPresent` becomes `False` even though the Python variable still holds a reference.

fontlab.flObject.isReleased.reference: `True` if this object has been released and its underlying C++ resources have been freed. Accessing properties on a released object is unsafe. Always check `isValid` before using an object you did not just create yourself.

fontlab.flObject.isValid.reference: The safest single validity check. Returns `True` if the object exists, is not null, and has not been released. Check this before using any object that might have been deleted by an earlier operation in your script.

fontlab.flObject.name.reference: The human-readable name of this object. For a glyph this is the glyph name; for a layer it is the master name; for a shape you can assign any label you like. Setting this property does not affect the object's unique `id`.

fontlab.flObject.refCnt.reference: The number of Python/C++ references currently holding onto this object. When `refCnt` drops to zero the object may be cleaned up. Primarily a debugging tool — you will rarely need to inspect this in production scripts.

fontlab.flObject.release.reference: Releases the internal reference this Python handle holds on the underlying C++ object. After calling this, the object may be garbage-collected if nothing else refers to it. You rarely need to call this explicitly — Python's reference counting handles cleanup.

fontlab.flObject.remove.reference: Removes this object from its parent container, or removes the given child object from this object. For example, calling `shape.remove()` removes it from its layer. This is the safe way to delete an object — it updates all internal bookkeeping.

fontlab.flObject.removeChild.reference: Removes a specific child object from this object's children list. Similar to `remove(child)` but makes the direction explicit — you are acting on a known parent and removing a known child.

fontlab.flObject.restoreHistoryState.reference: Rolls the object back to the history state at the given index. This is how you implement programmatic undo — get the current state index, subtract 1, and call this method.

fontlab.flObject.setFlag.reference: Sets flag `f` to `True` (or to the given boolean `value` if provided). Equivalent to turning a bit on. Call `setFlag(f, False)` to turn it off, which is the same as calling `clearFlag(f)`.

fontlab.flObject.setProperty.reference: Stores a value under the given key. The value can be a string, int, or float — it is stored as a QVariant. If a property with the same key already exists, its value is replaced.

fontlab.flObject.setPropertyFloat.reference: Stores a float value under the given key, using float-appropriate serialization. Prefer this over `setProperty` when storing coordinates, weights, or other decimal values, so retrieval with `getPropertyFloat` round-trips cleanly.

fontlab.flObject.setPropertyInt.reference: Stores an integer value under the given key. Use this for counters, indices, or any discrete numeric metadata so it round-trips cleanly with `getPropertyInt`.

fontlab.flObject.tag.reference: Gets or sets a short string tag on the object. Called with no argument it returns the current tag; called with a string it sets it. Tags are a quick labeling mechanism — similar to properties but without needing a key.

fontlab.flObject.type.reference: An integer constant identifying what kind of object this is. Every subclass (shape, node, layer, glyph, etc.) has its own type constant. Pass this value to `fl.flModel.typeToStr()` to get a human-readable name like `"Shape"` or `"Node"`.

fontlab.flObject.update.reference: Signals to FontLab that this object's data has changed and the UI should reflect the latest state. Call this after programmatic changes if the canvas or inspectors are not updating on their own.

fontlab.flObjectsList_flGuideLine_.reference:
These are native mutable object-list wrappers, used by APIs such as `flShapeData.includes`. They differ from a detached Python `list`. Their runtime names contain angle brackets, so they are not ordinary Python identifiers; if necessary, retrieve a type with `getattr(fontlab, "flObjectsList<flShape>")`.

Constructors accept no arguments, another compatible wrapper, an `flObject`, or a compatible Python sequence. They include the common flObject registrations.

Use the wrapper's mutation methods to edit its contents. Changing its `list` snapshot does not replace the native list. Referenced drawing objects remain model objects; a list snapshot does not clone them. Manage history and notifications when editing document-owned data.

fontlab.flObjectsList_flGuideLine_.appen.reference: Append an item of the wrapper's element type.

These are native mutable object-list wrappers, used by APIs such as `flShapeData.includes`. They differ from a detached Python `list`. Their runtime names contain angle brackets, so they are not ordinary Python identifiers; if necessary, retrieve a type with `getattr(fontlab, "flObjectsList<flShape>")`.

Constructors accept no arguments, another compatible wrapper, an `flObject`, or a compatible Python sequence. They include the common flObject registrations.

Use the wrapper's mutation methods to edit its contents. Changing its `list` snapshot does not replace the native list. Referenced drawing objects remain model objects; a list snapshot does not clone them. Manage history and notifications when editing document-owned data.

fontlab.flPackage.reference:
`flPackage` *is* your font file. Everything that makes up a font — every glyph, every master, the design-space axes, named instances, kerning tables, OpenType feature code, stems, alignment zones, guidelines, and all the metadata that ends up in the font's name tables — lives inside one `flPackage` object.

Inherits from `flObject`.

## What is a Package?

When you open a `.vfc`, `.ufo`, `.otf`, or any other supported format in FontLab, the application creates an `flPackage` for it. In a script, wrap the low-level current font with `fl.flPackage(fl.CurrentFont())`, after checking that `fl.CurrentFont()` is not `None`.

### The object hierarchy

It helps to picture the font as a set of nested containers:

```
flPackage  (the whole font)
 └── flGlyph  (one character — "A", "g", "comma", …)
      └── flLayer  (one drawing per master — "Regular", "Bold", …)
           └── flShape  (a group of contours, possibly a component reference)
                └── flContour  (one closed or open path)
                     └── flNode  (one on-curve or off-curve point)
```

Most scripting work moves through this hierarchy: you start at the font, find a glyph, pick a layer, iterate its shapes, and then walk the contours and nodes. Understanding this chain makes the API feel logical rather than arbitrary.

### Masters and variable fonts

In a variable font the `flPackage` acts as the top-level container and each **master** is a child `flPackage` stored in `font.variationPackages`. The master packages share glyph names and structure but hold different coordinate values. When FontLab interpolates, it travels this list and blends the numbers.

For a single-master font `variationPackages` has just one entry — the font itself.

### Kerning

Kerning in FontLab is stored per master. The `kerning(master_name)` method returns a dictionary of `{(glyph1, glyph2): value}` pairs for a specific master. When working with class kerning, the keys use group names prefixed with `@MMK_L_` and `@MMK_R_`.

### OpenType features

The OpenType feature code you write in the Features panel is stored in the `featuresContainer` inside the package. You can read and write feature code programmatically, which is useful for generating or validating feature files as part of a build pipeline.

## Common Patterns

### Getting the active font and listing its glyphs

```python
import fontlab as fl
font = fl.CurrentFont()
print(f"{font.info.familyName} — {font.glyphsCount} glyphs")
for g in font.glyphs:
    print(f"  {g.name}  u={hex(g.unicode) if g.unicode else '-'}")
```

### Changing font metadata

```python
font = fl.CurrentFont()
info = font.info
info.familyName   = "My Serif"
info.copyright    = "© 2026 My Foundry"
info.openTypeOS2WeightClass = 400
```

### Finding a glyph and navigating to its nodes

```python
font  = fl.CurrentFont()
glyph = font.findName("g")
layer = glyph.layers[0]
for shape in layer.shapes:
    for contour in shape.contours:
        for node in contour.nodes:
            print(node.x, node.y, node.type)
```

### Reading and setting a kern pair

```python
font        = fl.CurrentFont()
master_name = font.masters[0]   # e.g. "Regular"

# Read all kern pairs for this master:
pairs = font.kerning(master_name)
for (g1, g2), value in list(pairs.items())[:10]:
    print(f"  {g1} / {g2}  =  {value}")

# Set a specific pair:
font.setKerningPair(master_name, "A", "V", -40)
```

### Adding an axis to make a variable font

```python
from fontlab import flAxis
font = fl.CurrentFont()
wght = flAxis()
wght.name     = "Weight"
wght.tag      = "wght"
wght.minimal = 100
wght.maximum = 900
wght.default = 400
font.addAxis(wght)
```

## Tutorial

```python
from PythonQt.QtCore import QPointF
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import flPackage

# ============================================================
# 1. Opening and inspecting a font
# ============================================================

# fl.CurrentFont() gives you the flPackage for the active font.
# If no font is open it returns None, so check before using it.
font = fl.CurrentFont()
if font is None:
    print("No font is open!")
else:
    # font.info is a structured object with all UFO-compatible metadata.
    # It mirrors the keys in a UFO fontinfo.plist.
    print(f"Family: {font.info.familyName}")
    print(f"Style:  {font.info.styleName}")
    print(f"UPM:    {font.upm}")
    print(f"Glyphs: {font.glyphsCount}")
    print(f"Masters: {font.masters}")

# ============================================================
# 2. Iterating all open fonts
# ============================================================

# fl.AllFonts() returns every font currently open in FontLab.
# This is useful for batch operations across a whole family.
for f in fl.AllFonts():
    print(f"  Open font: {f.info.familyName} / {f.info.styleName}")

# ============================================================
# 3. Accessing and iterating glyphs
# ============================================================

font = fl.CurrentFont()

# Direct dictionary-style access by glyph name:
glyph_A = font['A']
print(f"Found '{glyph_A.name}' — width: {glyph_A.advanceWidth}")

# Find by name (returns None if not found — safer for scripting):
glyph_g = font.findName("g")
if glyph_g:
    print(f"Lowercase g: {glyph_g.advanceWidth} units wide")

# Find by unicode codepoint:
glyph_euro = font.findUnicode(0x20AC)   # €
if glyph_euro:
    print(f"Euro glyph: '{glyph_euro.name}'")

# Iterate every glyph:
empty_glyphs = []
for g in font.glyphs:
    if not g.hasBody:
        empty_glyphs.append(g.name)
print(f"Empty glyphs: {empty_glyphs}")

# ============================================================
# 4. Navigating the hierarchy: glyph → layer → shape → node
# ============================================================

# This is the most important pattern to understand.
# Everything lives inside everything else.

glyph   = font['H']
layer   = glyph.layers[0]          # first master layer
print(f"Layer '{layer.name}' has {len(layer.shapes)} shapes")

for shape in layer.shapes:
    for contour in shape.contours:
        print(f"  Contour: {len(contour.nodes)} nodes, "
              f"{'closed' if contour.closed else 'open'}")
        for node in contour.nodes:
            print(f"    ({node.x:.0f}, {node.y:.0f})  type={node.type}")

# ============================================================
# 5. Working with font-level guidelines
# ============================================================

from fontlab import flGuideLine

# Add a horizontal guideline at y=700 (e.g. for cap height):
gl = flGuideLine(0.0, QPointF(0, 700))
font.addGuideline(gl)

# List all font-level guidelines:
for guide in font.guidelines:
    print(f"Guide at angle={guide.angle}  pos={guide.centerPoint}")

# ============================================================
# 6. Masters in a variable font
# ============================================================

print(f"Masters: {font.masters}")
print(f"Active master: {font.master}")

# Switch to a different master:
if len(font.masters) > 1:
    font.setMaster(font.masters[1], notify=True)

# Read the design-space location of the active master:
loc = font.location()
print(f"Current location: {loc}")

# ============================================================
# 7. Editing font metadata
# ============================================================

info = font.info
print(f"Designer: {info.openTypeNameDesigner}")

# Write metadata — these end up in the font's name tables:
info.copyright              = "Copyright 2026 My Foundry"
info.openTypeOS2WeightClass = 400     # Regular weight
info.openTypeNameDesigner   = "Jane Smith"

# Font-level metrics (affects line spacing and hinting zones):
font.xHeight_value   = 500
font.capsHeight_value = 700
font.ascender_value  = 800
font.descender_value = -200

# ============================================================
# 8. Kerning
# ============================================================

master_name = font.masters[0]
pairs       = font.kerning(master_name)

# Print the first 5 kern pairs:
for (g1, g2), val in list(pairs.items())[:5]:
    print(f"  {g1} / {g2}  =  {val}")

# ============================================================
# 9. Saving
# ============================================================

# Save to the same location the font was opened from:
# font.save()

# Save to a new path:
# font.saveAs("/path/to/MyFont_v2.vfc")
```

## Current wrapper and naming helpers

`flPackage.hasInstaceFor(fg_font)` is the registered spelling, including the missing "n" in "Instance"; `hasInstanceFor` is not an alias. `clearActiveGlyphs()` clears the package's active-glyph collection. `checkVariableName(name)` returns the native checked variable-name string. `guidelinesHost` is a read-only `GuidelinesHostIntf` interface value when exposed by the build; it does not imply that `GuidelinesHostIntf` is a constructible module class.

### Guideline host property

| Property | Type | Access | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `guidelinesHost` | GuidelinesHostIntf | read | Native guideline-host interface. Its availability does not export a constructible module class of the same name. |

fontlab.flPackage.activateGlyph.reference: Open the given glyph in the glyph editor and make it active.

fontlab.flPackage.addAxis.reference: Add a design-space axis (e.g. Weight, Width). Returns the accepted axis name.

fontlab.flPackage.addGlyph.reference: Add a glyph to the font. The glyph must have a unique name; use `findNewName` if you're not sure.

fontlab.flPackage.addInstance.reference: Add a named instance to the font.

fontlab.flPackage.addMaster.reference: Add a new master to the font. If `create_glyphs=True`, empty glyph layers are created for every existing glyph. Pass a `source` package to copy layer data from it. Returns the accepted master name.

fontlab.flPackage.allGuidelines.reference: All guidelines including any special types.

fontlab.flPackage.ascender_value.reference: The ascender height — how far the tallest ascenders reach above the baseline, in font units.

fontlab.flPackage.assignData.reference: Copy all data from another package into this one. Overwrites everything.

fontlab.flPackage.autoKern.reference: Automatically calculate and set a kern value for a specific pair of glyphs in the given master.

fontlab.flPackage.autohintGlyphs.reference: Run FontLab's auto-hinting algorithm on a list of glyphs. Pass `make_hints=True` to actually write the hints; `False` just analyses without committing.

fontlab.flPackage.axes.reference: All design-space axes defined in this font.

fontlab.flPackage.bold.reference: `True` if this font is styled as bold. Sets the relevant OS/2 bits.

fontlab.flPackage.buildShapeDataNames.reference: Return a set of all unique shared shape data names in the font, excluding a given object. Useful for generating new unique names.

fontlab.flPackage.can_interpolate.reference: Return `True` if the font (or a specific master) is compatible for interpolation — meaning all glyphs have matching structure across masters.

fontlab.flPackage.capsHeight_value.reference: The cap height — the distance from baseline to the top of flat capital letters like "H".

fontlab.flPackage.caretOffset_value.reference: Horizontal offset for the text insertion caret in italic fonts.

fontlab.flPackage.checkAxisName.reference: Validate and potentially correct an axis name, ensuring it meets OpenType requirements.

fontlab.flPackage.clearMasters.reference: Remove all masters from the font. Pass `release=True` to also free the underlying memory. Destructive — use with care.

fontlab.flPackage.close.reference: Close the font. With no argument or `True`, prompt to save unsaved changes. Pass `False` to discard changes and close without prompting. Canceling the prompt leaves the font open.

fontlab.flPackage.collectNames.reference: Collect all glyph names into the storage descriptor before saving.

fontlab.flPackage.completeData.reference: Fill in any missing font information — default names, metrics, and flags — based on what is already set. Useful after programmatically building a font from scratch.

fontlab.flPackage.convertZonesToGuidelin.reference: Convert a set of alignment zones into font-level guidelines. Useful for visual reference while drawing.

fontlab.flPackage.cornerTension_value.reference: The global corner tension for smart corners.

fontlab.flPackage.counterAnchors.reference: The number of font-level anchor points defined.

fontlab.flPackage.currentSearch.reference: The serialised state of the current font-window search filter.

fontlab.flPackage.curveTension.reference: Global curve tension value — affects how FontLab draws Bézier curves.

fontlab.flPackage.defaultMaster.reference: The name of the master used as the interpolation origin (usually the "Regular" or middle weight).

fontlab.flPackage.deleteGlyph.reference: Remove a glyph from the font permanently. Returns `True` on success.

fontlab.flPackage.deleteGroups.reference: Delete one or more groups. If `deleteDependentContent=True`, also removes kerning pairs that depended on those groups.

fontlab.flPackage.descender_value.reference: The descender depth — a negative number for how far descenders drop below the baseline.

fontlab.flPackage.elidedName.reference: A shortened family name used when the full name is too long for some environments.

fontlab.flPackage.ensureProteusData.reference: Ensure that FontLab's Proteus-specific metadata block is initialised on this package.

fontlab.flPackage.family_zones.reference: Return the family-level alignment zones, which apply across all masters.

fontlab.flPackage.family_zonesB.reference: Family-level bottom zones, shared across all masters.

fontlab.flPackage.family_zonesT.reference: Family-level top zones, shared across all masters.

fontlab.flPackage.featuresContainer.reference: Return the container holding the OpenType feature code.

fontlab.flPackage.ffn.reference: Full font name — the complete name as it appears in font menus, e.g. `"Gill Sans Bold Italic"`.

fontlab.flPackage.fgId.reference: The low-level fontgate integer identifier for this font.

fontlab.flPackage.fgPackage.reference: The underlying low-level fontgate font object.

fontlab.flPackage.fileName.reference: Just the filename without its directory path.

fontlab.flPackage.findAxis.reference: Find an axis by its full name, or `None` if not found.

fontlab.flPackage.findAxisShort.reference: Find an axis by its four-letter OpenType tag (e.g. `"wght"`, `"wdth"`).

fontlab.flPackage.findFgId.reference: Find a glyph by its internal low-level integer id. Rarely needed in scripts.

fontlab.flPackage.findGroup.reference: Find a group by its integer id.

fontlab.flPackage.findName.reference: Find and return the glyph with the given name, or `None`. The fastest and most common way to look up a glyph by name.

fontlab.flPackage.findNameId.reference: Find a glyph by its fontgate name id. Rarely needed in scripts.

fontlab.flPackage.findNewName.reference: Given a proposed name, return a version that is guaranteed to be unique in this font (e.g. `"A.alt2"` if `"A.alt"` is already taken).

fontlab.flPackage.findShapeRoot.reference: Find the glyph that owns (defines) a particular shared shape data.

fontlab.flPackage.findStem.reference: Find a stem by name and return its index in the stem list, or `-1` if not found. Pass `loose=True` for a fuzzy name match.

fontlab.flPackage.findUnicode.reference: Find the glyph assigned to a given unicode codepoint. Pass the integer value, e.g. `0x0041` for "A".

fontlab.flPackage.findZone.reference: Find a zone by name and return its index. `top` specifies whether to search top or bottom zones.

fontlab.flPackage.fontLayerOrder.reference: The ordered list of master names, which determines master order in interpolation.

fontlab.flPackage.generateGlyph.reference: Build a composite glyph from a recipe string (e.g. `"A+acutecomb"`). Returns a list of component descriptors and the calculated advance width.

fontlab.flPackage.getAccentsInfo.reference: Return accent-positioning information for a given anchor point on a layer. Used internally when building composite glyphs.

fontlab.flPackage.getAllGroups.reference: Return all glyph groups (kerning classes and general groups) with full metadata. Each entry is a tuple of group type flag, name, id, mark colour, and member glyph names.

fontlab.flPackage.getAxisName.reference: Given a four-letter tag, return the full axis name.

fontlab.flPackage.getAxisShortName.reference: Given a full axis name, return its four-letter tag.

fontlab.flPackage.getLayerName.reference: Return the name of the currently active master layer.

fontlab.flPackage.getMarkOffset.reference: Compute the positional offset between matching anchors in two glyphs on the named layer. Returns `None` if no matching anchors are found.

fontlab.flPackage.getShapes.reference: Return the ids of all shared shapes whose names match the filter string.

fontlab.flPackage.glyphsCount.reference: The total number of glyphs in the font.

fontlab.flPackage.hasAxis.reference: Return `True` if an axis with that name exists.

fontlab.flPackage.hasAxisShort.reference: Return `True` if an axis with that four-letter tag exists.

fontlab.flPackage.hasGuides.reference: Return `True` if there are any font-level guidelines defined.

fontlab.flPackage.hasInstaceFor.reference: Check whether a Python `flPackage` wrapper already exists for the given low-level font. Prevents creating duplicate wrappers.

fontlab.flPackage.hasMaster.reference: Return `True` if a master with that name exists in this font.

fontlab.flPackage.hasName.reference: Return `True` if a glyph with that name already exists. Pass `relaxed=True` for a case-insensitive check.

fontlab.flPackage.hasPackageHistoryStora.reference: Check whether the undo history goes back at least to the given index.

fontlab.flPackage.hasWeightAxis.reference: `True` if the font has a weight axis defined in its design space.

fontlab.flPackage.hasWidthAxis.reference: `True` if the font has a width axis defined.

fontlab.flPackage.hasZones.reference: Return `True` if there are any alignment zones defined.

fontlab.flPackage.info.reference: The structured font info object — gives you access to all UFO-compatible metadata fields like `familyName`, `styleName`, `copyright`, and OS/2 values.

fontlab.flPackage.initItr.reference: Initialise the TrueType interpreter for this font. Required before running the TT hint engine.

fontlab.flPackage.initItrGlyph.reference: Initialise the TT interpreter for a specific glyph, loading its outline data into the interpreter's memory.

fontlab.flPackage.inktrapLen_value.reference: The ink-trap length for optical corrections at sharp joins.

fontlab.flPackage.instanceAttributes.reference: Default layer attributes for generated instances.

fontlab.flPackage.instances.reference: All named instances (the specific points in design space you've chosen to name).

fontlab.flPackage.interpolateInstance.reference: Generate a fully interpolated font package at the given design-space location. Pass `round=True` to quantise all coordinates to integers.

fontlab.flPackage.interpolateMaster.reference: Compute an interpolated master layer at the given location and write the result into the named master.

fontlab.flPackage.interpolationCheckGeom.reference: Whether FontLab verifies that master outlines have compatible geometry before interpolating.

fontlab.flPackage.interpolationExtrapola.reference: Whether interpolation is allowed to extrapolate beyond the defined axis range.

fontlab.flPackage.interpolationFlags.reference: A bit-field of options that control how interpolation behaves for this font.

fontlab.flPackage.interpolationMutatorMa.reference: Whether to use the MutatorMath engine for interpolation (more powerful than simple linear blending).

fontlab.flPackage.interpolationSortConto.reference: Whether FontLab sorts contours by position before interpolating (helps avoid crossed outlines).

fontlab.flPackage.isComponent.reference: Check whether a shape data is used as a component. If it is, returns the source glyph and the transform applied to it.

fontlab.flPackage.isKey.reference: `True` if this package is the key (default) master in a variable font project.

fontlab.flPackage.isMaster.reference: `True` if this package is a master font within a variable font.

fontlab.flPackage.italic.reference: `True` if this font is styled as italic.

fontlab.flPackage.italicAngle_value.reference: The italic angle in degrees. Negative for a standard right-leaning italic, e.g. `-12.0`.

fontlab.flPackage.keepShapeData.reference: When `True`, shared shape data is preserved on export rather than expanded to individual outlines.

fontlab.flPackage.kerning.reference: Return the kerning table for the given master as a dictionary. Keys are `(left, right)` name tuples; values are integer kern amounts in font units.

fontlab.flPaper.reference:
Metrics view background layer.

## What is flPaper?

The "paper" is the background layer of the metrics view canvas. It is the model object that manages the ordered list of all `flGlyphInfo` objects currently being rendered — the glyphs that are shown in the text string of the metrics/spacing view. It also tracks which glyph is the "active" one (the one whose outline nodes are currently visible and editable).

In typical scripting you access the paper through the canvas rather than creating one directly. The paper is your gateway to understanding what is being displayed: which glyphs are on screen, which is selected for editing, and what the combined bounding rectangle of all displayed content is.

## Tutorial

`flPaper` is the object you use to ask "what is on screen right now, and which glyph is active?" in the metrics view.

```python
import fontlab as fl

# ============================================================
# Access the paper of the current metrics/glyph window canvas
# and inspect what is displayed.
# ============================================================

ws     = fl.flWorkspace.instance()
canvas = ws.getActiveCanvas()
if canvas is None:
    print("Open a glyph or metrics window first.")
    raise SystemExit

paper = canvas.paper
if paper is None or not paper.hasContent():
    print("Paper has no content — type something in the metrics view.")
    raise SystemExit

print(f"Paper has content: {paper.hasContent()}")
print(f"Active glyph open: {paper.hasActive()}")

# Get the bounding box of all displayed glyphs in canvas units:
bounds = paper.glyphsBoundRect()
print(f"All-glyphs canvas bounds: "
      f"({bounds.left():.0f}, {bounds.top():.0f}) → "
      f"({bounds.right():.0f}, {bounds.bottom():.0f})")

# Get the active glyph info:
if paper.hasActive():
    gi = paper.activeGlyphInfo()
    print(f"Active glyph: '{gi.name}'")

# ============================================================
# Iterate all glyphs currently displayed on the paper.
# ============================================================

# The paper's glyphInfoAt(i) API requires knowing the count.
# Use the canvas's glyphInfos() shortcut if available,
# otherwise iterate with a try-except:
print("\nGlyphs on paper:")
i = 0
while True:
    try:
        gi = paper.glyphInfoAt(i)
        if gi is None:
            break
        print(f"  [{i}] '{gi.name}'")
        i += 1
    except Exception:
        break

# ============================================================
# Programmatically open a glyph for editing in the metrics view.
# ============================================================

font  = paper.package()
glyph = font['O']
new_gi = paper.setActiveGlyph(glyph)
if new_gi:
    print(f"\nOpened '{new_gi.name}' for editing.")
    fl.Update()
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Check if a specific glyph is currently in the text string

```python
import fontlab as fl

ws     = fl.flWorkspace.instance()
canvas = ws.getActiveCanvas()
if canvas:
    paper = canvas.paper
    font  = fl.CurrentFont()
    if paper and font:
        gi = paper.getGlyphInfo(font['a'])
        if gi:
            print("'a' is on the paper.")
        else:
            print("'a' is not currently displayed.")
```

### Zoom the canvas to show all glyphs

```python
import fontlab as fl

ws     = fl.flWorkspace.instance()
canvas = ws.getActiveCanvas()
if canvas:
    paper = canvas.paper
    if paper and paper.hasContent():
        rect = paper.glyphsBoundRect()
        canvas.centerOnRect(rect)   # or use canvas.zoomToRect(rect)
        fl.Update()
```

fontlab.flPaper.activeGlyphInfo.reference: Returns the `flGlyphInfo` of the glyph that is currently active — the one shown with its outline nodes. Returns `Nothing` if no glyph is active. Cast to `flGlyphInfo` before use.

fontlab.flPaper.createInstance.reference: Creates a detached `flPaper` instance. In most use cases the paper is created and managed by the canvas engine.

fontlab.flPaper.getGlyphInfo.reference: Given an `flGlyph`, returns its `flGlyphInfo` on this paper if it is currently displayed. Returns `Nothing` if the glyph is not in the current text string.

fontlab.flPaper.glyph.reference: Returns the main `flGlyph` currently displayed (the active glyph, if set).

fontlab.flPaper.glyphInfoAt.reference: Returns the `flGlyphInfo` at position `index` in the paper's ordered list. Use this with `hasContent()` and a known count to iterate all displayed glyphs.

fontlab.flPaper.glyphsBoundRect.reference: Returns the bounding rectangle in canvas units that encloses all displayed glyphs. Useful for computing a "zoom to fit" level or checking which area needs repainting.

fontlab.flPaper.hasActive.reference: Returns `True` if one of the displayed glyphs is currently active (its outline nodes are visible and editable). When no glyph is open for editing, returns `False`.

fontlab.flPaper.hasContent.reference: Returns `True` if the paper has at least one glyph to display. An empty paper (empty text string) returns `False`.

fontlab.flPaper.package.reference: Returns the `flPackage` (font file) whose glyphs are displayed on this paper.

fontlab.flPaper.setActiveGlyph.reference: Sets which glyph is open for outline editing (shows its nodes). Returns the updated `flGlyphInfo`. Use this to programmatically open a glyph for editing in the metrics view.

fontlab.flPaper.setPaperGlyph.reference: Sets which glyph is the main (central) glyph displayed on the paper. Returns the new `flGlyphInfo` for that glyph.

fontlab.flPinPoint.reference:
Named anchor for mark positioning.

## What is an anchor?

Anchors — represented in code as `flPinPoint` objects — are the small triangular markers you place on glyphs to tell FontLab how combining marks (like accents, dots, and cedillas) connect to base letters. If you've ever placed a "top" anchor on a lowercase *a* and a "_top" anchor on an acutecomb, you've been working with `flPinPoint`.

The system works by pairing anchors that share the same name, one from a base letter and one from a mark:

- An anchor **without** a leading underscore (e.g. `top`, `bottom`, `ogonek`) lives on the **base letter**. It says: *"This is the spot where a combining mark can attach to me."*
- An anchor **with** a leading underscore (e.g. `_top`, `_bottom`, `_ogonek`) lives on the **combining mark**. It says: *"This is my attachment point — align me here when connecting to a base."*

When FontLab (or the OpenType shaping engine) needs to position acutecomb on top of *a*, it looks for a `top` anchor on the *a* and a `_top` anchor on the acutecomb, then positions the mark so those two points coincide.

Common anchor names you'll encounter:
- `top` / `_top` — for marks that sit above a letter (acute, grave, circumflex, etc.)
- `bottom` / `_bottom` — for marks below (cedilla, ogonek)
- `ogonek` / `_ogonek` — for the ogonek diacritic specifically
- `horn` / `_horn` — for the Vietnamese horn marks

### Cloud mode

When you enable **cloud mode** on an anchor, the anchor's position is no longer fixed to absolute coordinates. Instead, FontLab calculates its position dynamically from the nearest point on the glyph's outline. This is useful for anchors on glyphs whose shapes vary significantly across masters in a variable font — the cloud anchor "floats" to an optically correct position at each master rather than staying locked to coordinates that might be wrong at extreme instances.

### Expression anchors

Like guidelines, anchors can have their X and Y coordinates driven by arithmetic expressions. For example, you can set `expressionX = "=lsb + (rsb - lsb) / 2"` to always place an anchor at the horizontal center of a glyph's advance width, no matter how wide the glyph gets.

## flPinPoint vs flAnchor — what's the difference?

This is a common point of confusion. There are **two anchor classes** in FontLab:

- **`flPinPoint`** (Python name: `flPinPoint`) — the named anchor that lives on a glyph layer and participates in mark-to-base positioning. This is the one you create, name, and inspect when building an OpenType mark feature. It's what you see as the little triangle in the glyph editor.

- **`flAnchor`** — a lower-level geometric link that connects a shape to a guideline or another shape within FontLab's composite/smart-corner system. You don't create these by hand; they appear on `shape.anchors()` as part of FontLab's internal shape-attachment mechanism. They store references to the attached objects (node, shape, guideline) and record which movement directions are constrained. Unless you're doing advanced shape scripting or building smart components, you'll rarely need to touch `flAnchor` directly.

In short: if you're building mark-to-base or mark-to-mark positioning, work with `flPinPoint`. If you're exploring how shapes lock to each other in composites, you might encounter `flAnchor`.

## Tutorial

Anchors are the most reliable way to position diacritics and combining marks. Here is the complete workflow: adding anchors to a base letter, adding anchors to a mark, and verifying the pairs.

```python
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import flPinPoint

# Use the native Python class name:
flPinPoint = fl.flPinPoint

font = fl.CurrentFont()

# ============================================================
# Step 1: List existing anchors on a glyph.
# ============================================================

glyph = font['a']
if glyph is None:
    print("No 'a' glyph in this font.")
    raise SystemExit

layer = glyph.layers[0]
print(f"Anchors on '{glyph.name}':")
for anchor in layer.anchors:
    expr = f"  (formula: x={anchor.expressionX}, y={anchor.expressionY})" \
           if anchor.hasExpression else ""
    print(f"  '{anchor.name}': ({anchor.point.x():.0f}, {anchor.point.y():.0f}){expr}")

# ============================================================
# Step 2: Add a 'top' anchor to a base letter.
# Place it at the top center of the glyph's bounding box.
# ============================================================

bbox  = layer.boundingBox()
top_x = (bbox.left() + bbox.right()) / 2
top_y = bbox.top()

existing_names = {a.name for a in layer.anchors}
if 'top' not in existing_names:
    top_anchor = flPinPoint(top_x, top_y)
    top_anchor.name = "top"
    layer.addAnchor(top_anchor)
    print(f"\nAdded 'top' anchor at ({top_x:.0f}, {top_y:.0f})")
    fl.Update()
else:
    print("\n'top' anchor already exists — skipping.")

# ============================================================
# Step 3: Add the corresponding '_top' anchor to a mark glyph.
# The mark anchor should be at its attachment point (usually
# the bottom of the accent shape).
# ============================================================

mark_glyph = font['acutecomb']
if mark_glyph:
    mark_layer = mark_glyph.layers[0]
    mark_bbox  = mark_layer.boundingBox()
    attach_x   = (mark_bbox.left() + mark_bbox.right()) / 2
    attach_y   = mark_bbox.bottom()   # bottom of accent = attachment point

    mark_names = {a.name for a in mark_layer.anchors}
    if '_top' not in mark_names:
        mark_anchor = flPinPoint(attach_x, attach_y)
        mark_anchor.name = "_top"
        mark_layer.addAnchor(mark_anchor)
        print(f"Added '_top' anchor to 'acutecomb' at ({attach_x:.0f}, {attach_y:.0f})")
        fl.Update()

# ============================================================
# Step 4: Use an expression anchor for the center-top position.
# This anchor always stays at the horizontal center regardless
# of the glyph width.
# ============================================================

center_anchor = flPinPoint(0, 0)
center_anchor.name       = "top"
center_anchor.expressionX = "=(lsb + rsb) / 2 + width / 2"
center_anchor.expressionY = "=xHeight"
print(f"\nExpression anchor: x='{center_anchor.expressionX}'"
      f"  y='{center_anchor.expressionY}'")
print(f"Has expression: {center_anchor.hasExpression}")
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

### Add top/bottom anchors to all lowercase letters

```python
import fontlab as fl

flPinPoint = fl.flPinPoint
font   = fl.CurrentFont()

LOWERCASE = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'

for char in LOWERCASE:
    glyph = font[char]
    if glyph is None:
        continue
    layer = glyph.layers[0]
    bbox  = layer.boundingBox()
    cx    = (bbox.left() + bbox.right()) / 2

    existing = {a.name for a in layer.anchors}

    if 'top' not in existing:
        a = flPinPoint(cx, bbox.top()); a.name = "top"
        layer.addAnchor(a)

    if 'bottom' not in existing:
        a = flPinPoint(cx, bbox.bottom()); a.name = "bottom"
        layer.addAnchor(a)

fl.Update()
print(f"Added top/bottom anchors to {len(LOWERCASE)} glyphs.")
```

### Find all anchor name pairs (base + mark)

```python
import fontlab as fl

font       = fl.CurrentFont()
base_names = set()
mark_names = set()

for glyph in font.glyphs:
    for layer in glyph.layers:
        for anchor in layer.anchors:
            if anchor.name.startswith("_"):
                mark_names.add(anchor.name[1:])
            else:
                base_names.add(anchor.name)

pairs   = base_names & mark_names
orphans = (base_names | mark_names) - pairs
print(f"Paired anchor names: {sorted(pairs)}")
print(f"Unpaired:            {sorted(orphans)}")
```

Use the `flPinPoint.PinPointStyle` dictionary with subscription.

| Key | Native value | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `FreePosition` | `flPinPoint::PinPointStyle::FreePosition` | Native enum value. |
| `ShapeBound` | `flPinPoint::PinPointStyle::ShapeBound` | Native enum value. |

Inherited binding members: flObject.

fontlab.flPinPoint.anchor.reference: When `True`, this is a mark attachment anchor for mark-to-base positioning. When `False`, it is a metrics or reference point.

fontlab.flPinPoint.appearance.reference: Visual style index controlling how this anchor is drawn in the editor. Different values produce different triangle styles or sizes.

fontlab.flPinPoint.cloudEnabled.reference: Enables glyph construction, automatic positioning, Anchor Clouds, and live Mark Attachment preview. Turning this off also clears `markEnabled`; turning it back on does not restore mark participation.

fontlab.flPinPoint.createInstance.reference: Allocates and returns a new, empty anchor instance.

fontlab.flPinPoint.expressionX.reference: Arithmetic expression controlling the anchor's X position. Use font metric names as variables: `"=lsb"`, `"=rsb"`, `"=xHeight * 0.5"`, etc.

fontlab.flPinPoint.expressionY.reference: Arithmetic expression for the anchor's Y position. Works the same way as `expressionX`.

fontlab.flPinPoint.hasExpression.reference: `True` if either `expressionX` or `expressionY` is set. Check this before reading expressions.

fontlab.flPinPoint.isLatch.reference: `True` if this anchor is in latch (locked) mode — snapped to and held at a specific contour position.

fontlab.flPinPoint.markEnabled.reference: Enables participation in generated OpenType `mark` and `mkmk` features. Requires `cloudEnabled`. Setting this to `True` while cloud is off leaves mark disabled.

fontlab.flPinPoint.name.reference: The anchor's name — what pairs anchors between base letters and marks. Use `"top"` on a base and `"_top"` on a mark to create a mark-to-base relationship.

fontlab.flPinPoint.point.reference: The anchor's position in font units. Read with `.point.x()` and `.point.y()`, or assign a new `QPointF` to move it.

fontlab.flPinPoint.style.reference: The display style enum for this pin-point. Related to `appearance`.

fontlab.flPinPoint.translate.reference: Moves the anchor by the given offset vector. For example, `translate(QPointF(0, 10))` nudges the anchor 10 units upward.

fontlab.flPreferences.reference:
`flPreferences` gives scripts **read and write access to almost every setting** in FontLab — the same settings you'd normally change in the Preferences dialog. You can read them to understand the current working environment, or write them to temporarily change FontLab's behavior for the duration of your script.

You always access preferences through the singleton:

```python
from fontlab import flPreferences
prefs = flPreferences.instance()
```

**A word of caution:** Changes to preferences take effect **immediately and globally**. If your script changes a preference, it stays changed even after the script finishes — the user's environment is affected. For settings you change temporarily, always save the original value and restore it when you're done:

```python
prefs = flPreferences.instance()

# Save original
old_snap = prefs.snapToGuidelines

# Change for your script
prefs.snapToGuidelines = False

# ... do your scripted work ...

# Restore original
prefs.snapToGuidelines = old_snap
```

After changing any preferences, call `flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()` so all panels and displays pick up the new values.

## Window-opening preferences

| Property | Type | Access | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `generalActivateFontWindowOnOpen` | bool | read/write | Activate the Font window when opening a font; off by default. |
| `generalHideWarningDialogs` | bool | read/write | Suppress optional launch/opening dialogs; off by default. See behavior below. |

## Active window when reopening a font

`generalActivateFontWindowOnOpen` is a read/write boolean, **off by default**.
When off, opening a font with saved windows returns to its saved active window.
This also applies when saving glyph-window contents without panel/window layout.
Older files use their saved selected tab when available, or preserve the window activated by
the restoration order when no active-window information exists. Set it to `True` to
activate the Font window instead:

```python
flPreferences.instance().generalActivateFontWindowOnOpen = True
```

Window restoration must be enabled to restore a saved active window.

## Suppressing launch and font-opening dialogs

`generalHideWarningDialogs` is a read/write boolean, off by default, corresponding to **Preferences > General > Other > Hide warning dialogs**:

```python
from fontlab import flPreferences
prefs = flPreferences.instance()
prefs.generalHideWarningDialogs = True
```

The change takes effect immediately and is saved for subsequent launches. Set it to `False` to restore dialogs. It suppresses startup prompts (including crash reporting and Welcome), font-opening warnings, legacy note encoding conversion, and Important Font Note dialogs. Pending crash reports are sent automatically without dialogs; failed uploads are retained for retry. Autosaved fonts are moved to the Keep folder without reopening them. Automatic update checks are suspended while enabled; license restrictions still apply.

Imports follow the configured rounding preference. Optional repairs (merging/renaming elements, renaming masters, removing linked width expressions) and encoding conversion are skipped. Required duplicate-glyph-name and cross-layer-reference repairs still run, with messages in Output. Font collections open all faces. Known damaged autosaves and Sketchboards are skipped without deletion. Opening errors are reported in Output instead of a dialog.

For temporary use, save and restore the value with `try`/`finally`. MCP exposes the same setting as `general.hide_warning_dialogs` through `get_preferences` and `set_preferences`.

## Getting the Instance

```python
from fontlab import flPreferences
prefs = flPreferences.instance()
print(prefs.editorNodeSize)   # read a value
prefs.editorNodeSize = 8      # write a value
```

## Common Scripting Patterns

```python
from fontlab import flPreferences, flItems

prefs = flPreferences.instance()

# --- Read a value ---
print("Node size:", prefs.editorNodeSize)

# --- Change a value (always save the original first!) ---
orig = prefs.editorNodeSize
prefs.editorNodeSize = 8
# ... do your work ...
prefs.editorNodeSize = orig   # restore

# --- Notify the app after changes ---
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()

# --- Save/restore a full preferences snapshot ---
snapshot = prefs.save()
prefs.editorFillOpacity = 0   # make glyphs transparent
# ... do proofing work ...
prefs.load(snapshot)          # restore everything
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()

# --- Temporarily disable all snapping ---
snap_props = ['snapToGrid', 'snapToGuidelines', 'snapToOutline',
              'snapToBounds', 'snapToMetrics']
orig_snaps = {p: getattr(prefs, p) for p in snap_props}
for p in snap_props:
    setattr(prefs, p, False)
# ... do work without snapping ...
for p, v in orig_snaps.items():
    setattr(prefs, p, v)
```

## Tutorial

```python
from PythonQt.QtGui import QColor
import fontlab as fl
from fontlab import flPreferences, flItems

# ============================================================
# 1. Get the preferences singleton
# ============================================================

prefs = flPreferences.instance()
print("Preferences loaded. Dark mode:", prefs.isDark)
print("Data path:", prefs.dataPath)

# ============================================================
# 2. Reading preferences
# ============================================================
# These are just attribute reads — safe, no side effects.

print("\n--- Editor display ---")
print(f"  Node size: {prefs.editorNodeSize} px")
print(f"  Fill opacity: {prefs.editorFillOpacity}%")
print(f"  Show curve handles: {prefs.editorShowCurves}")
print(f"  Show coordinates: {prefs.editorCoordinates}")

print("\n--- Nudge distances ---")
print(f"  Arrow key nudge: {prefs.editorNudge1} units")
print(f"  Shift+arrow nudge: {prefs.editorNudge10} units")

print("\n--- Snap settings ---")
print(f"  Snap to guidelines: {prefs.snapToGuidelines}")
print(f"  Snap to outline: {prefs.snapToOutline}")
print(f"  Snap distance: {prefs.editorSnapDistance} px")

print("\n--- Grid ---")
print(f"  Grid X: {prefs.gridDistanceX}, Grid Y: {prefs.gridDistanceY}")
print(f"  Grid opacity: {prefs.gridOpacity}")

# ============================================================
# 3. Safely changing a preference
# ============================================================
# ALWAYS save the original value so you can restore it.
# Never leave preferences in a changed state when your
# script finishes, unless that's the explicit goal.

orig_node_size = prefs.editorNodeSize

print(f"\nChanging node size from {orig_node_size} to 10...")
prefs.editorNodeSize = 10

# Tell the app to refresh all displays with the new value
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()

# ... do some work where larger nodes are helpful ...

# Restore
prefs.editorNodeSize = orig_node_size
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()
print("Node size restored.")

# ============================================================
# 4. Saving and restoring a full preferences snapshot
# ============================================================
# prefs.save() returns a dict of all current preference values.
# prefs.load(dict) restores from that dict.
# Use this to make large temporary changes safely.

snapshot = prefs.save()
print(f"\nSaved preferences snapshot ({len(snapshot)} entries).")

# Make some temporary changes for a proofing workflow:
prefs.editorFillOpacity = 0        # transparent fill
prefs.editorShowCurves  = False     # hide handles
prefs.editorCoordinates = False     # hide coordinate display
prefs.colorWorkspace    = QColor(240, 240, 240)   # light grey background
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()

print("Temporary proofing preferences applied.")
print("(In a real script, do your proofing work here.)")

# Restore everything from the snapshot
prefs.load(snapshot)
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()
print("Preferences fully restored from snapshot.")

# ============================================================
# 5. Temporarily disabling all snapping
# ============================================================
# Useful before running a layout script where snapping
# would interfere with programmatic positioning.

snap_props = [
    'snapToGrid', 'snapToGuidelines', 'snapToFontGuidelines',
    'snapToFontMetrics', 'snapToMetrics', 'snapToOutline',
    'snapToBounds', 'snapToCenters', 'snapToDistance'
]

# Save originals
orig_snaps = {p: getattr(prefs, p) for p in snap_props}

# Disable all snapping
for p in snap_props:
    setattr(prefs, p, False)
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()
print("\nAll snapping disabled.")

# ... run your positioning script here ...

# Restore all snap settings
for p, v in orig_snaps.items():
    setattr(prefs, p, v)
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()
print("Snap settings restored.")

# ============================================================
# 6. Configuring grid spacing
# ============================================================
# For a 1000-unit UPM font, a 10-unit grid is common.
# setGridDistances() sets both axes at once.

orig_gx = prefs.gridDistanceX
orig_gy = prefs.gridDistanceY

flPreferences.setGridDistances(10.0, 10.0)
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()
print(f"\nGrid set to 10×10 (was {orig_gx}×{orig_gy}).")

# Restore
flPreferences.setGridDistances(orig_gx, orig_gy)
flItems.notifyPreferencesChanged()

# ============================================================
# 7. Reading the data path (where scripts and resources live)
# ============================================================

print(f"\nFontLab data path: {prefs.dataPath}")
print(f"Default data path: {prefs.dataPathDefault}")
print(f"Auto-save path: {prefs.pathAutoSave}")

# ============================================================
# 8. Checking dark mode
# ============================================================
# Scripts that generate colours can adapt to the current theme.

if prefs.isDark:
    bg_colour = QColor(30, 30, 30)
    fg_colour = QColor(220, 220, 220)
    print("\nDark mode: using light-on-dark colours.")
else:
    bg_colour = QColor(255, 255, 255)
    fg_colour = QColor(0, 0, 0)
    print("\nLight mode: using dark-on-light colours.")

print("\nPreferences tutorial complete.")
```

fontlab.flPreferences.colorEncoding.reference: The colour used for encoding indicators (Unicode assignment markers).

fontlab.flPreferences.colorFontCell.reference: The background colour of glyph cells in the font window.

fontlab.flPreferences.colorGrid.reference: The colour of grid lines in the glyph editor.

fontlab.flPreferences.colorKerning.reference: The colour used to display kerning pairs in the metrics window.

fontlab.flPreferences.colorMask.reference: The colour of the mask overlay in the glyph editor.

fontlab.flPreferences.colorMaskGlobal.reference: The colour of the global mask overlay.

fontlab.flPreferences.colorMaskLocal.reference: The colour of the local (glyph-level) mask overlay.

fontlab.flPreferences.colorMetrics.reference: The colour of metrics lines (baseline, cap height, x-height, etc.) in the editor.

fontlab.flPreferences.colorMetricsLines.reference: The colour of secondary metrics lines.

fontlab.flPreferences.colorWorkspace.reference: The background colour of the workspace canvas area.

fontlab.flPreferences.convertDetectZoneT.reference: When converting from PS to TT (or vice versa), automatically detect alignment zone tags.

fontlab.flPreferences.convertPostScriptP.reference: How precisely curves are fitted when converting to PostScript cubic format. Higher values = closer fit, more nodes.

fontlab.flPreferences.convertTrueTypePre.reference: How precisely curves are fitted when converting to TrueType quadratic format.

fontlab.flPreferences.convertTrueTypeSho.reference: Use the short-curve optimization in TrueType output — this creates shorter, more efficient curve data but may slightly alter curve shapes.

fontlab.flPreferences.dataPath.reference: The path to the FontLab user data directory — where scripts, brushes, and other user resources are stored.

fontlab.flPreferences.dataPathDefault.reference: The factory-default data path. This is the path FontLab ships with and cannot be overridden.

fontlab.flPreferences.defaultTexts.reference: The list of default sample text strings used in the Metrics and Text windows.

fontlab.flPreferences.doInterpolate.reference: Returns whether variable font interpolation is currently enabled.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorAcrossGlyphs.reference: Allow editing operations (like node dragging) to span across multiple glyphs in the metrics view.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorAcrossLayers.reference: Allow operations to affect multiple master layers simultaneously.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorAcrossShapes.reference: Allow operations to span multiple shapes within a glyph.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorClickSelects.reference: Whether clicking directly on a curve segment selects it (and its nodes).

fontlab.flPreferences.editorContrast.reference: Enhance outline contrast for better visibility against the background.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorCoordinates.reference: Whether to show coordinate values next to selected nodes.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorCoordinatesE.reference: Whether coordinate values shown next to nodes can be edited inline by clicking.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorCurvatureSiz.reference: The size of curvature comb spines. Larger = more prominent combs.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorDarkPreview.reference: Use a dark background in Preview mode (simulates dark-on-light rendering).

fontlab.flPreferences.editorDirectKernin.reference: Enable direct kerning mode — allows dragging sidebearings to adjust kerning in the metrics view.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorDragInactive.reference: Whether inactive shapes can be dragged without first activating them.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorFastPreview.reference: Use faster but lower-quality preview rendering. Useful for performance on large glyphs.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorFillOpacity.reference: The opacity of the glyph fill colour in the editor, as a percentage (0 = transparent, 100 = solid).

fontlab.flPreferences.editorFillOpenCont.reference: Fill open contours with colour in the editor (so they look like closed paths even when they aren't).

fontlab.flPreferences.editorFixedBCP.reference: Keep off-curve control points at fixed positions when moving their on-curve neighbor. When `False`, off-curve points follow the on-curve point proportionally.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorFrameSelects.reference: When using frame (rubber-band) selection, only capture nodes whose on-curve point is inside the frame. When `False`, nearby off-curve points are also included.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorGuideHitDist.reference: How close the cursor needs to be to a guideline to click and select it, in screen pixels.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorInactiveHand.reference: Show Bézier handles for shapes that are not currently the active/selected shape.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorInactiveNode.reference: How inactive (non-selected-shape) nodes are displayed: 0 = hidden, other values = different rendering modes.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorInactiveWire.reference: Display inactive shapes as wireframe outlines rather than filled shapes.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorInertion.reference: Enable inertia scrolling (the view continues to scroll after you lift your finger).

fontlab.flPreferences.editorKeyboardJoin.reference: Allow joining open contour endpoints using a keyboard shortcut.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorLayerDoubleC.reference: Double-clicking on a glyph activates its layer for editing.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorMetricsDoubl.reference: Double-clicking in the metrics window enters edit mode for that glyph.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorNodeColor.reference: The colour scheme for nodes — an index into FontLab's built-in node colour palettes.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorNodeSize.reference: The size of node circles in the editor, in screen pixels. Typical range: 4–12. Larger values make nodes easier to click, especially at lower zoom levels.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorNudge1.reference: The small nudge distance — the amount moved per arrow key press. Usually 1 font unit.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorNudge10.reference: The large nudge distance — the amount moved with Shift + arrow key. Usually 10 font units.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorOutlineThick.reference: The thickness of the outline stroke drawn around glyph contours in the editor, in pixels.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorScrollBars.reference: Show scroll bars in the glyph editor.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorShiftConstra.reference: The Shift key constrains movement to horizontal or vertical axes.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorShiftExtends.reference: Shift-clicking adds to the current selection rather than replacing it.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorShowCoordina.reference: Controls coordinate display mode for selected nodes.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorShowCurves.reference: Whether to show Bézier curve handles (the "arms" extending from smooth nodes).

fontlab.flPreferences.editorShowNodeName.reference: Controls whether node names are shown (0 = never, other values = various display modes).

fontlab.flPreferences.editorSnapDistance.reference: How close (in screen pixels) the cursor needs to be to a snap target for snapping to activate. Typical values: 4–12.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorTopBottom.reference: Show top and bottom metrics lines (ascender/descender) in the editor.

fontlab.flPreferences.editorUndoSelectio.reference: Include selection state in the undo history (so undoing an edit also restores the previous selection).

fontlab.flPreferences.editorZoomAscender.reference: When switching to a new glyph in the editor, automatically zoom to fit the ascender height.

fontlab.flPreferences.exportConflictMode.reference: What to do when an export file already exists: 0 = overwrite, 1 = ask, etc.

fontlab.flPreferences.exportContent.reference: What to include in the export (all glyphs, only glyphs with outlines, etc.).

fontlab.flPreferences.exportDestinationF.reference: The default folder path where exported font files are saved.

fontlab.flPreferences.exportDestinationM.reference: Where exported files go: 0 = same folder as source, 1 = specified folder, etc.

fontlab.flPreferences.exportJsonContours.reference: Include contour data in JSON format exports.

fontlab.flPreferences.exportJsonFormatti.reference: Pretty-print (format with indentation) JSON exports for readability.

fontlab.flPreferences.exportSaveVFJ.reference: Automatically save a VFJ (JSON font) copy alongside the exported binary font.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontAbsentGray.reference: Grey out glyph cells for glyphs that don't have outlines (absent from the current layer).

fontlab.flPreferences.fontAllGlyphs.reference: Show all glyphs regardless of the current encoding — useful for seeing the full glyph inventory.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontAuditTests.reference: Returns the list of audit test IDs that are currently enabled.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontCaptionEditabl.reference: Allow glyph names to be edited inline by clicking the caption under each cell.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontCaptionHeight.reference: The height in pixels of the caption row below each glyph cell.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontColoredCaption.reference: Use colour for glyph name captions (based on glyph mark colour).

fontlab.flPreferences.fontColoredItems.reference: Colour-code glyph cells based on their mark colour.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontMarkBright.reference: Use brighter, more saturated mark colours.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontMarkOpacity.reference: The opacity of glyph mark colour overlays in the font window (0–255).

fontlab.flPreferences.fontNameUnicode.reference: Show Unicode codepoint values alongside glyph names in the font window.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontNoteIcon.reference: Show a small note icon in glyph cells that have notes attached.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontNoteText.reference: Show the note text directly inside glyph cells.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontShowGlyphMetri.reference: Show metrics values (advance width etc.) in each glyph cell.

fontlab.flPreferences.fontUnicodeName.reference: Display glyph names as their Unicode alias names (e.g. "LATIN SMALL LETTER A" instead of "a").

fontlab.flPreferences.gridDistanceX.reference: Horizontal grid spacing in font units. For a 1000-unit UPM, common values are 10, 20, or 50.

fontlab.flPreferences.gridDistanceY.reference: Vertical grid spacing in font units.

fontlab.flPreferences.gridItalicAngle.reference: Tilt the grid by the font's italic angle, so the grid aligns with the slant of italic letters.

fontlab.flPreferences.gridOpacity.reference: The opacity of grid lines (0.0–1.0). 0 = invisible, 1 = fully opaque.

fontlab.flPreferences.gridPointOpacity.reference: The opacity of grid intersection dots (0.0–1.0).

fontlab.flPreferences.gridSlant.reference: A manual slant angle for the grid, in degrees. Used when `gridItalicAngle` is `False` but you want a custom-angled grid.

fontlab.flPreferences.hintMaxH.reference: Maximum number of horizontal hints allowed per glyph during auto-hinting.

fontlab.flPreferences.hintMaxV.reference: Maximum number of vertical hints per glyph.

fontlab.flPreferences.hintMinH.reference: Minimum horizontal stem width (in font units) that the auto-hinter will generate a hint for.

fontlab.flPreferences.hintMinV.reference: Minimum vertical stem width for auto-hinting.

fontlab.flPreferences.historyStoreSelect.reference: Include selection state in the undo history — undo steps will also restore what was selected.

fontlab.flPreferences.historyStoreViewPo.reference: Include the scroll position in the undo history — undo steps restore the view position too.

fontlab.flPreferences.importComponents.reference: Keep composite components when importing — `True` preserves components, `False` decomposes them on open.

fontlab.flPreferences.importConvertCurve.reference: Automatically convert curve types (TT↔PS) when importing fonts.

fontlab.flPreferences.importDecompileFea.reference: Decompile binary OpenType features into source code on import.

fontlab.flPreferences.importDecompose.reference: Decompose all composites to plain contours on import.

fontlab.flPreferences.importRoundCoordin.reference: Round all coordinates to integer values on import.

fontlab.flPreferences.inactiveMastersOpa.reference: The opacity (0.0–1.0) of inactive master layer overlays shown in the glyph editor.

fontlab.flPreferences.interpolateSmartRo.reference: Use smart rounding when interpolating variable font masters — produces cleaner integer coordinates.
